title: Preoperative optimization for ventral hernia repair: augmented evidence review
authors: Moustafa F, Fafaj A, Petro C, Blackman MH, Blake KE
abstract: Augmented evidence review (AER) integrating three evidence streams to answer what the key components of preoperative optimization for ventral hernia repair are: empiric (retrospective Abdominal Core Health Quality Collaborative analysis), social media (International Hernia Collaboration surgeon survey), and artificial intelligence — OpenEvidence performed a data-driven literature review. Obesity associated with increased wound complications but not systemic complications; diabetes/glycemic control not associated with complications; smoking associated with surgical site occurrence and pneumonia. Most surgeons favor individualized approaches (obesity > smoking > diabetes). AI-derived evidence demonstrated similar heterogeneity to surgeon practice.
relevance: First AER-framework paper using OpenEvidence as the AI evidence stream — OE's data-driven literature review treated as one of three independent evidence sources in peer-reviewed surgical research.
key_findings: OpenEvidence performed the AI-driven literature review stream of the AER
AI-derived evidence showed similar heterogeneity to practicing surgeons' optimization practices
Obesity linked to wound complications; smoking to SSO/pneumonia; diabetes not significant
Cleveland Clinic / UTHSC group — establishes AER methodology with OE built in
scale: ACHQC retrospective cohort + IHC survey

title: Trends in Inguinal Hernia Repair Approach: An Augmented Evidence Review
authors: Head WT, Kalsotra S, Satija D, Renshaw S, Collins CE, Poulose B
abstract: First evaluation of inguinal hernia repair (IHR) trends using the novel 'Augmented Evidence Review' (AER) framework integrating three evidence streams: (1) empiric — ACHQC registry, 2766 initial IHR (1777 open vs 989 MIS) and 294 recurrent IHR (142 open vs 152 MIS), 2016-2023; (2) social media — International Hernia Collaboration poll (474 responses); (3) artificial intelligence — OpenEvidence used to synthesize peer-reviewed literature. MIS utilization rose 20.2% (initial) and 18.0% (recurrent), driven by robot-assisted repair; laparoscopy declined. OpenEvidence corroborated the shift with published guidelines and studies; divergences centered on robotic vs laparoscopic platform preference and the Alternate-Plane Principle in recurrent repairs.
relevance: Second paper in J Gastrointest Surg's AER series using OpenEvidence as a formal research evidence stream (alongside registry data and surgeon surveys) — institutionalizes OE as a literature-synthesis instrument in surgical research methodology.
key_findings: OpenEvidence served as the AI evidence stream in a three-stream Augmented Evidence Review
OE output corroborated registry and survey findings (shift to MIS/robotic IHR) with cited guidelines
AER framework proposed as a reusable research methodology — OE embedded by design
MIS inguinal hernia repair up ~20% in both initial and recurrent settings, robot-assisted primary driver
scale: ACHQC n=3,060 patients; IHC poll n=474 surgeons

title: Responsible and innovative AI for mental health care: five priority themes
authors: Paulus MP, Torous J, Perlis RH, Sarma KV, Ajilone O, Khalsa SS, Rodriguez CI
abstract: ACNP 2026 study group synthesis on translating AI into clinical mental health care. Argues barriers are now infrastructural (measurement, governance, evidence standards) rather than computational. Five priorities: (1) robust measurement/phenotyping infrastructure; (2) clinician-facing augmentation tools (ambient documentation, structured decision-support pipelines) as the most immediate scalable impact; (3) patient-facing AI requires rigorous safety evaluation, esp. implicit suicide risk and heterogeneous treatment effects; (4) governance/equity frameworks beyond privacy (bias, digital literacy, research integrity); (5) move from predictive to causal/mechanistic precision psychiatry.
relevance: High-profile academic agenda-setting for clinical AI decision support in psychiatry; explicitly names clinician-facing CDS/decision-support pipelines as the highest-impact near-term use case — the category OpenEvidence occupies. Safety-evaluation priority (suicide risk) reinforces the case for OE-style safety benchmarking.
key_findings: ACNP study group: AI's clinical impact in psychiatry constrained by infrastructure, not model capability
Clinician-facing augmentation (ambient docs, decision-support pipelines) = most immediate scalable impact
Patient-facing AI needs rigorous safety evaluation, particularly for implicit suicide risk
Governance must extend beyond privacy to bias, digital literacy, research integrity
Calls for causal/mechanistic approaches over purely predictive models
scale: ACNP study group synthesis (2026)

title: Performance of large language models in data extraction for evidence synthesis: A systematic review
authors: Shankar R, Lim A, Qian X
abstract: Systematic review of 27 studies (PROBAST+AI, TRIPOD-LLM assessed) evaluating LLMs for systematic-review data extraction through Dec 2025. Models included GPT-4/4o (n=15), Claude 2-3.5 (n=10), Gemini (n=3), open-source (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek). Overall accuracy 47-99.9%. Claude 3.5 Sonnet 91.0% > human-only 89.0%. Omissions dominant error (60-74%); hallucinations only 0.08-6%. Time savings 33-87%.

title: Diagnostic Ambiguity in Appendicitis: Comparing Failure Modes of Large Language Models and Surgeons
authors: Çalışkan YK, Başak F, Erdem O, Kudaş İ
abstract: Comparative cross-sectional diagnostic-accuracy simulation using 150 standardized emergency-department vignettes (90 appendicitis, 60 non-surgical mimics enriched for diagnostically difficult scenarios). Six frontier AI systems and two board-certified general surgeons evaluated each vignette using a fixed triage prompt. GPT-5 achieved highest accuracy (95.3%) exceeding GPT-4o (82.0%; P<0.001) and slightly surpassing specialist consensus (92.7%). In pediatric/geriatric vignettes GPT-5 93.8% vs specialists 90.0% vs GPT-4o 71.2%. Identified distinct failure modes including search-induced hallucinations in web-augmented systems.

Identifies distinct failure modes including search-induced hallucinations in web-augmented systems

150 standardized emergency-department vignettes; 6 frontier AI systems vs 2 board-certified general surgeons

title: Correct but Incomplete: Limitations of AI-Assisted Decision Support in Rectal Cancer
authors: Meyer RJ, Bresler TE, Makaryan TT, Gheissari R, Mauch A, Fujita M
abstract: Evaluated ChatGPT-5 (OpenAI) and OpenEvidence against NCCN Guidelines for Rectal Cancer (Version 2.2025). 138 clinical scenarios across workup/diagnosis, treatment, and surveillance. Two physicians scored on 5-point Likert for Correctness (≥3) and Accuracy (≥4). ChatGPT-5: Correct 98.6%, Accurate 84.1%; OpenEvidence: Correct 92.8%, Accurate 81.2%. Overall Correctness favored ChatGPT-5 (P=0.035); Accuracy showed no significant difference (P=0.634). Both ≥90% Correctness across all domains. Defines appropriate role of AI as adjunct to (not substitute for) multidisciplinary review.

authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Behavioral audit of how medical LLMs use patient evidence when generating diagnoses. Reveals that diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used case evidence appropriately — even high-accuracy models can use evidence in clinically inappropriate ways.

title: Biological Amnesia in ICU Time-Series Prediction: A Drift-Adaptive Two-Stream Architecture with Temporal Retrieval
authors: Fatema Ferdous Tamanna, K. M. Merajul Arefin, Md. Abdul Masud
abstract: Clinical decision support systems degrade silently as treatment protocols evolve because standard adaptation methods treat models as monolithic blocks, unable to distinguish stable patient physiology from shifting institutional practice. We propose an adaptive clinical intelligence architecture for ICU intervention prediction that structurally decouples physiological from treatment representations, confining parameter updates to the treatment stream upon a dual distributional and accuracy trigger. Automated audit logs record which treatment features drove each adaptation event and how their importance shifted. At inference, an attribution-driven Temporal RAG module grounds each prediction in patient-specific, era-matched PubMed evidence anchored to the patient's dominant physiological features. Experiments used 84,792 MIMIC-IV stays (2008-2022) under strict chronological split. Drift localised entirely to the treatment stream, validating the structural prior. Selective adaptation improved vasopressor and septic shock discrimination and calibration over the static source model. A fully retrained baseline missed 26 septic shock cases the framework correctly identified, with none in the reverse direction; retrieval consistency with the pre-adaptation source model was preserved by the framework but degraded substantially in the retrained baseline.
relevance: ICU-level CDSS with adaptive temporal RAG — directly addresses clinical AI drift in point-of-care decision support, with strong MIMIC-IV evaluation and medical-record-grounded retrieval
key_findings: Structural decoupling confined drift entirely to treatment stream while preserving physiological representations
Selective adaptation improved vasopressor and septic shock discrimination and calibration
Framework correctly identified 26 septic shock cases that a fully retrained baseline missed (no false positives in reverse)
Retrieval consistency with pre-adaptation source model preserved; degraded substantially in retrained baseline
Architecture offers template for governable, interpretable adaptive clinical AI deployment
scale: 84,792 MIMIC-IV ICU stays (2008-2022)

title: Quality of Tinnitus Information From Generative AI Systems and Web Search: An Expert-Rated Comparative Study
authors: Hack S, Tessler I, Saltz D, Hayu D, Henry JA, Sanda G, Boldes T, Wolfovitz A, Horn DL, Zalzal HG, Aaron KA
abstract: Comparative study evaluating tinnitus-related information quality from 6 GenAI systems (OpenEvidence, Claude, DeepSeek, GPT-5, Gemini, GPT-4) and Google Search. 30 common tinnitus questions from US Google Trends (2020-2025) rated by 6 experts using QAMI framework across 5 domains (accuracy, clarity, relevance, completeness, usefulness). OpenEvidence achieved the highest mean score (4.45±0.72), followed by Claude (4.00±1.02), DeepSeek (3.92±1.13), GPT-4 (3.89±0.84), Gemini (3.62±0.98), and GPT-5 (3.30±1.11). Google Search scored lowest (2.27±1.12). Completeness was the lowest-performing domain across systems. OpenEvidence showed significant differences vs all other systems (effect size r=0.49-0.86). Inverse relationship between expert-rated quality and readability — OpenEvidence had postgraduate-level readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade 17.5) while general-purpose LLMs produced 6th-7th grade level responses.
relevance: Directly evaluates OpenEvidence against 5 other GenAI systems and web search for patient-facing clinical information quality

OpenEvidence significantly outperformed all other systems with large effect sizes (r=0.49-0.86)

title: MedFailBench: A Clinician-Built Open-Source Benchmark for Medical AI Safety Boundary Inspection
authors: Goktug Ozkan
abstract: Most medical AI benchmarks measure whether a model knows the correct answer. MedFailBench asks a different question: which safety boundary failed? A clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1-5) and safety gate type: missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap. Contains 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs. Released under Apache-2.0 and CC-BY-4.0.

title: MamaBench: Benchmarking LLM Robustness in Maternal and Child Health Diagnosis through Counterfactual Clinical Perturbation
authors: Thanni Adewuyi, Anuoluwa Sotome, Samuel Okoko, Angel Ezendu, Oluwafunke Akinbuwa, Oluwaseun Odunsi, Oluwasegun Oguntuase, Oluwadarasimi Oguntuase, Ifeoma Nwabueze, Abiodun Adereni
abstract: First counterfactual benchmark for maternal and paediatric AI: 434 expert-authored clinical narratives in 217 pairs across 371 pathologies, evaluated via the Bias Trap Rate (BTR) — the conditional probability that a model fails the counterfactual given success on the base case. Proposes Evidence-Anchored RAG (EA-RAG), a three-stage retrieval method replacing aggregate similarity with an evidence coverage objective. Across eight configurations of four frontier LLMs, base accuracy overstates robust accuracy by 16-28 percentage points. EA-RAG achieves 20.3% BTR and 65.0% robust accuracy on Claude Sonnet 4.6, a 5.5 percentage point BTR reduction without degrading base accuracy. Residual 20% BTR confirms counterfactual robustness in clinical AI remains an open challenge.

title: X-FEMR: Token-level Explainability for Electronic Health Records Foundation Models
authors: Jie Huang, Pengfei Yin, Zihan Xu, Daniel Capurro, Mike Conway, Ting Dang
abstract: Foundation Models for Electronic Health Records (FEMRs) are pretrained on large-scale structured patient data, enabling them to convert longitudinal patient trajectories into generalizable representations for diverse clinical prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, FEMRs remain black-box models, raising concerns about bias, interpretability, and clinical trust. We propose the first token-level explainability approach for FEMRs. We train a Transformer-based surrogate model on input-output pairs from the FEMR across two prediction tasks, approximating its behavior while preserving temporal dynamics. We identify the most influential tokens, providing insights into how FEMRs leverage different aspects of patient history. To evaluate clinical relevance, we introduce a novel clinical alignment metric that quantifies the correspondence between the surrogate model's key tokens and clinically validated features. Results demonstrate that the surrogate closely approximates FEMR predictions and that token-level explanations align well with clinical knowledge, offering a practical framework for interpretable and trustworthy clinical AI.

title: Clinician-Level Agreement Without Clinical Caution: LLM Evaluator Limits in Medical AI Benchmarking
authors: William Philipp, Finn Fassbender, Thorsten Langer, Martje Pauly, Rebecca Herzog, Alexander Baumann, Markus Hobert, Theresa Paulus, Ip Chi Wang, Lukas Goede, Johanna Reimer, Sebastian Löns, Ronald Böck, Sebastian Fudickar
abstract: Open-response evaluation provides stronger clinical validity than multiple-choice benchmarks but creates a scoring bottleneck that motivates automated LLM-as-a-Judge approaches. We introduce MedQADE, the first standardized open-response clinical benchmark for German, comprising 3,800 items annotated by ten practicing physicians and nine LLM evaluators. The top-performing evaluator (Gemini 3 Flash) reached alignment consistent with the physician ceiling (kappa=0.694 vs kappa=0.709), but automated evaluators exhibited near-absent clinical metacognition: physicians scaled abstention with item difficulty, while frontier models assigned definitive scores in every case. Systematic lineage-dependent biases found models preferentially scored architectural siblings.
relevance: Evaluates limits of LLM-as-judge approaches in medical AI benchmarking — critical context for interpreting all benchmark results using automated evaluators
key_findings: LLM evaluators can achieve statistical alignment with physician ceiling but lack clinical metacognition
Physicians scaled abstention with item difficulty; frontier models assigned definitive scores in every case
Systematic lineage-dependent biases: models preferentially scored architectural siblings
Statistical alignment does not ensure clinical caution
Evaluator independence requires explicit verification
scale: 3,800 items, 10 practicing physicians, 9 LLM evaluators

title: Readable but Not Controllable: Neuron-Level Evidence for Medical LLM Hallucination
authors: Vijay Vankadaru, Asha Matthews, Tanya Roosta, Peyman Passban
abstract: Studies hallucination in medical LLMs at neuron level. Probe achieves AUROC 0.77-0.86 for detection. Hallucination signal is distributed and redundant. Sharp gap between decodability and controllability - same structure that makes hallucination detectable does not enable reliable neuron-level control. Suggests hallucination mitigation requires more than identifying right neurons.
relevance: Directly addresses clinical AI safety - hallucination detection and control in medical LLMs
key_findings: Probe reliably detects hallucination with AUROC 0.77-0.86
Hallucination signal is distributed and redundant, not narrowly localized
Sharp gap between decodability and controllability of hallucination
Neuron-level steering does not reliably correct hallucination
tools_evaluated: 4 open-source models across medical QA datasets
scale: 4 models, multiple medical QA datasets, 16 model-dataset combinations

title: Expert Evaluation of Clinical AI Tools on Real Point-of-Care Clinical Queries (Real-POCQi)
authors: Jean Feng et al.
abstract: Blinded evaluation built on 620 real-world Point-of-Care Queries (Real-POCQi) submitted to OpenEvidence by physicians across 30 specialties, plus 187 HealthBench questions. 149 physicians in specialty-matched head-to-head comparisons. OpenEvidence outperformed Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.5 on real-world clinical questions, contradicting the June Nature Medicine paper.
relevance: Directly contradicts the Nature Medicine study showing generalist LLMs beat clinical tools. Uses real-world queries from OpenEvidence platform.
key_findings: OpenEvidence outperformed Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.5 on real-world clinical questions
149 physicians in specialty-matched comparisons vs 12 clinicians in earlier study
Results contradict June 2026 Nature Medicine paper
Methodological distinction: head-to-head specialist matching vs isolated rubric scoring
scale: 620 real-world queries + 187 HealthBench, 149 physicians, 30 specialties

title: Primary ICD Category Prediction using LLM-based Probing
authors: Chengyuan Liu, Xinyue Zhang, Yao Li, Guanting Chen
abstract: ICD codes are central to reimbursement, research, and population health surveillance, yet automated coding systems often struggle to integrate diagnostic signals from both clinical narratives and structured electronic health record (EHR) variables. We evaluated whether frozen medical large language model (LLM) representations can serve as a shared embedding space for multimodal primary diagnosis category prediction. Frozen medical LLM representations are tested as a shared embedding space integrating clinical narratives and structured EHR variables for multimodal ICD coding.
relevance: Evaluates frozen medical LLMs as shared embedding space for multimodal ICD prediction — relevant to clinical AI billing/coding infrastructure and upstream of quality measurement
key_findings: Medical LLMs provide a shared embedding space across clinical narratives and structured EHR variables
Frozen LLM representations enable multimodal primary diagnosis category prediction without task-specific fine-tuning
Approach relevant to automated coding for reimbursement, research, and population health surveillance
scale: Multimodal EHR + clinical narrative corpus for ICD prediction

title: IMCBench: A benchmark for multimodal LLMs in Image-grounded Medical Conversations
authors: Maria Xenochristou, Ashutosh Joshi, Korosh Vatanparvar, et al.
abstract: Image-grounded, multi-turn medical conversation benchmark pairing real clinical images with synthetic patient profiles. Evaluates safety, accuracy, and appropriate use of uncertainty. Benchmarks 8 multimodal frontier models across 4 model families. Claude Opus 4.6 achieves highest score (3.61). Safety degrades for malignant and rare conditions. Visual input and EHR context contribute to safe guidance.
relevance: Medical AI benchmark for multimodal clinical conversations - evaluates safety and accuracy across frontier models
key_findings: Claude Opus 4.6 highest overall (3.61/5)
Safety degrades for malignant (-0.27) and rare conditions (-0.27)
Visual input removal drops safety by 0.18, EHR context removal by 0.23
Accurate clinical description does not guarantee safe patient guidance
scale: 8 multimodal frontier models, clinical images with synthetic patient profiles

title: Clinical Harness for Governable Medical AI Skill Ecosystems
authors: Tianhan Xu, Lei Bao, Zhe Hu, Tian Shen, Yongxiang Wang
abstract: Runtime governance architecture for clinical AI skills. Registers, orchestrates, constrains, and monitors clinical AI skills. Uses osteoporosis as exemplar showing how knowledge-driven, data-driven, and physics-enhanced skills can support lifecycle care. Provides governed substrate for future medical agents.
relevance: Clinical AI governance and safety framework - addresses safe deployment of clinical AI skills
key_findings: Defines clinical AI skills as governed, persistent capabilities
Runtime governance architecture for registering, orchestrating, constraining AI skills
Osteoporosis exemplar demonstrates lifecycle care support
Provides substrate for future medical AI agents
scale: Framework paper with osteoporosis case study

title: A Pipeline for Generating Longitudinal Synthetic Clinical Notes Using Large Language Models
authors: William Poulett, Alice Waterhouse, Ben Wallace, Scarlett Kynoch, Amaia Imaz Blanco
abstract: Pipeline and dataset for generating longitudinal synthetic clinical notes — privacy-preserving training/evaluation data for clinical AI tools in regulated settings where real patient data is restricted. Combines structured patient generation, semi-structured patient journey simulation, and unstructured clinical note generation. Designed to support clinical AI evaluation without privacy risk.
relevance: Synthetic longitudinal clinical-note generation pipeline for privacy-preserving clinical AI training and evaluation; complements existing clinical AI benchmarks lacking temporal data
key_findings: Modular pipeline: structured patient generation → semi-structured patient journey simulation → unstructured clinical notes
Privacy-preserving — avoids real patient data
Designed to support clinical AI tool training and evaluation
Longitudinal structure addresses gap in benchmarks that use isolated single-encounter cases
scale: Pipeline and dataset for clinical AI evaluation

title: Comparison of Large Language Model-Based Systems and Prompt Engineering for Internal Medicine Clinical Pharmacy Cases
authors: Yang SS et al.
abstract: Comparison of LLM-based systems and prompt engineering approaches for internal medicine clinical pharmacy cases.
relevance: Pharmacy-specific AI evaluation with prompt engineering comparison
key_findings: Compares LLM systems and prompt engineering for pharmacy cases
scale: Internal medicine pharmacy cases

title: MedBench v5: A Dynamic, Process-Oriented, and Hallucination-Aware Benchmark for Clinical Multimodal Models
authors: Jinru Ding, Chuchu Jiang, Lu Lu, et al.
abstract: Redesigned benchmark for clinical multimodal models moving from static QA to dynamic, process-oriented evaluation. Dual-dimensional framework: Clinical Cognitive Responsiveness (13 sub-dimensions) and Medical Atomic Skills (4 agent environments, 63 tasks). Three switchable stressors for factorized degradation analysis. Dynamic process audit protocol with 5 reasoning nodes. Hallucination propagation monitoring.
relevance: Comprehensive clinical AI benchmark with hallucination detection and process-oriented evaluation
key_findings: 63 tasks across 4 agent environments and 13 clinical sub-dimensions
Strong overall performance does not guarantee process stability
Stressors disrupt contradiction detection, diagnosis updating, hallucination propagation
Silent hallucination captured through 4 interaction stages
tools_evaluated: Frontier multimodal models (language, vision-language, agent systems)
scale: 63 tasks, 13 sub-dimensions, 4 agent environments

title: RASC+: Retrieval-Constrained LLM Adjudication for Clinical Value Set Authoring
authors: Sumit Mukherjee
abstract: Clinical value sets define the standardized terminology codes used in quality measurement, phenotyping, cohort construction, and clinical decision support. The recently introduced Retrieval-Augmented Set Completion (RASC) benchmark showed that direct zero-shot large language model (LLM) generation is poorly suited to this task: clinical code systems are large, version-controlled, and not reliably present in model pretraining. We propose RASC+, a retrieval-constrained adjudication pipeline that combines curated retrieval with constrained LLM reasoning to improve the reliability of value set authoring. RASC+ uses retrieval to constrain LLM generation to candidate codes present in real code systems, then adjudicates among candidates with explicit evidence-gathering and audit trails. The approach delivers higher-quality value sets with auditable provenance — directly relevant to healthcare organizations deploying clinical decision support, quality measurement, and EHR phenotyping.
relevance: Retrieval-constrained LLM pipeline for clinical value set authoring — upstream of CDSS quality measurement, EHR phenotyping, and cohort construction used in clinical AI systems
key_findings: Direct zero-shot LLM generation is poorly suited to clinical value set construction (large, version-controlled code systems)
RASC+ retrieval-constrained adjudication combines curated retrieval with constrained LLM reasoning
Pipeline delivers higher-quality value sets with auditable provenance
Supports CDSS, quality measurement, and EHR phenotyping infrastructure
scale: Clinical code systems value set evaluation (RASC benchmark extension)

title: Cohort-Anchored Foundation Models for EHR: Audit-Ready Risk Scores and Peer Cohorts
authors: Kaiping Zheng
abstract: Foundation models have achieved remarkable performance across medical question answering, imaging, and electronic health record (EHR) tasks, yet reliable clinical deployment remains challenging due to limited interpretability, vulnerability to distribution shift, and weak alignment with clinician reasoning. We argue that these limitations arise because existing approaches prioritize representation quality over clinical alignment, and propose cohort-anchored foundation models that produce audit-ready risk scores grounded in auditable peer cohorts. The framework reframes EHR-based predictions around clinician-facing cohort comparisons and structured audit trails — directly relevant to governance, regulatory, and physician-AI teaming requirements for clinical AI deployment.
relevance: Proposes cohort-anchored EHR foundation models with audit-ready risk scores and peer cohorts — directly addresses clinical AI governance and physician-facing alignment
key_findings: Existing EHR FMs prioritize representation quality over clinical alignment
Cohort-anchored framework reframes predictions around clinician-facing peer cohort comparisons
Produces audit-ready risk scores with structured audit trails
Addresses interpretability, distribution shift, and clinician-AI alignment for governance
tools_evaluated: Peer cohort comparison + audit trail generation
scale: Framework / methodology (no single benchmark scale reported)

title: Evaluation of ChatGPT, Gemini, and OpenEvidence in Obstetric and Gynecologic Clinical Decision Scenarios
authors: Atay AO et al.
abstract: Head-to-head comparison of ChatGPT, Gemini, and OpenEvidence in OB/GYN clinical decision scenarios.
relevance: Direct comparison of OpenEvidence against ChatGPT and Gemini in OB/GYN
key_findings: Three major AI tools compared in OB/GYN scenarios
scale: OB/GYN clinical decision scenarios

title: MedRLM: Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence for Long-Context Clinical Reasoning, Sensor-Guided Screening, Evidence-Grounded Decision Support, and Community-to-Tertiary Referral Optimization
authors: Aueaphum Aueawatthanaphisut
abstract: Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence framework for long-context clinical reasoning. Treats patient case as external clinical environment that can be recursively inspected, decomposed, retrieved, verified, and synthesized. Coordinates specialized agents for clinical text, longitudinal EHR, medical imaging, sensor signals, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, and referral planning. Clinical Evidence Graph Memory connects patient observations with retrieved evidence.
relevance: RAG-based clinical decision support framework with multimodal reasoning and agent coordination
key_findings: Recursive inspection of patient cases as external clinical environment
Specialized agents for text, EHR, imaging, sensors, guidelines, uncertainty, referral
Clinical Evidence Graph Memory connects observations with evidence
Sensor-guided recursive triggering for abnormal physiological patterns
scale: Framework paper with evaluation design using public and credentialed datasets

title: Machine Learning Classification of Cryopathy Syndromes: A Comprehensive Comparative Study
authors: Nataliya Shakhovska, Valentyna Chopyak, Ivan Izonin, Vira Haievska
abstract: Comparative study developing and evaluating ML approaches for automated classification of cryopathy syndromes from laboratory data to reduce dependence on expert judgment. Analyzed 2,686 patients across 14 diagnostic categories. Cryoglobulin-related tests are routinely difficult to classify because laboratory patterns overlap across rare and common categories; supports clinical decision support in a domain with limited expert availability.
relevance: Direct clinical-AI decision-support evaluation using ML classification on 2,686 lab records across 14 cryopathy-syndrome categories — addresses overlap between rare and common categories
key_findings: 2,686 patient records across 14 diagnostic categories
Identifies practical ML strategy for clinical decision support in cryopathy syndromes
Addresses expert-judgment bottleneck in classifying cryoglobulin-related tests
Comparative ML approaches for classification of rare and overlapping syndrome categories
scale: 2,686 patient records; 14 cryopathy-syndrome categories

title: Language Models as Interfaces, Not Oracles: A Hybrid LLM-ML System for Pediatric Appendicitis
authors: Soheyl Bateni, Maryam Abdolali
abstract: Hybrid system (ClaMPAPP) using LLM as interface rather than decision-maker. Extracts schema-constrained features from narratives, passes to XGBoost classifier. Evaluated on two independent pediatric appendicitis cohorts. LLM-as-interface design outperformed end-to-end LLMs while minimizing missed appendicitis cases. End-to-end LLMs showed unstable sensitivity-specificity trade-offs.
relevance: Clinical decision support using LLM as interface for structured ML prediction - safety-focused design pattern
key_findings: LLM-as-interface, ML-as-predictor design outperforms end-to-end LLMs
Minimizes missed appendicitis cases (key safety concern in acute triage)
End-to-end LLMs showed unstable sensitivity-specificity trade-offs
Greater degradation under narrative reordering for end-to-end LLMs
scale: Two independent pediatric appendicitis cohorts from German hospitals

title: PhysAssistBench: Are LLMs Ready to Assist Physicians? Interactive Doctor-Patient-EHR Assistance
authors: Tianming Du, Peijie Yu, Sihan Shang, et al.
abstract: Benchmark for interactive doctor-patient-EHR assistance. Built from real MIMIC-IV cases with agentic patients that turn static EHR records into multi-turn clinical scenarios. 1,296 manually reviewed and physician-validated turns. Current models remain unreliable - reliable assistance requires coordination across knowledge, communication, and systems.
relevance: Physician-AI teaming benchmark - directly evaluates clinical AI assistant readiness for real-world clinical workflows
key_findings: Current models remain unreliable for interactive clinical assistance
Reliable assistance requires coordination across knowledge, communication, and systems
1,296 physician-validated turns from real MIMIC-IV cases
Exposes key bottleneck: coordination across capabilities, not isolated gains
scale: 1,296 manually reviewed and physician-validated turns, real MIMIC-IV cases

title: AIPatient Arena: EHR-grounded evaluation of large language models in end-to-end clinical consultation workflows
authors: Jiahui Niu, Huizi Yu, Wenkong Wang, et al.
abstract: EHR-grounded evaluation framework for LLMs across 8 dimensions of clinical competence. Integrates EHR data into patient-specific knowledge graphs for multi-turn physician-patient interactions. 437 patients in primary cohort, 119 and 67 in OOD validation cohorts. Persistent weaknesses in handling ambiguous responses, information coverage, and diagnostic accuracy. Process-based evaluation reveals recurrent interaction failures.
relevance: Clinical AI benchmark for end-to-end consultation workflows - evaluates clinical competence dimensions
key_findings: LLMs performed well in questioning skills and ethics (4.43-4.99/5)
Persistent weaknesses in handling ambiguity (2.57-3.32/5), information coverage (2.08-3.02/5), diagnostic accuracy (2.63-3.55/5)
Recurrent failures: repetitive questioning, omission of medical history, inadequate uncertainty handling
Final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating clinical readiness
scale: 437 primary cohort patients, 119 + 67 OOD validation patients, 8 competence dimensions

title: Treatment Response Optimized Clinical Decision Support AI System via Digital Twin Simulation
authors: Xinyu Qin, Anil K. Sood, Ruiheng Yu, et al.
abstract: Online adaptive framework integrating Treatment Effect estimation, patient Digital Twin simulation, and Reinforcement Learning for sequential decision-making. Rule-based safety module blocks contraindicated treatments. Cases with model disagreement flagged for clinician review. Validated on synthetic simulator and real-world ovarian cancer dataset from TCGA. Superior effectiveness vs baselines with low latency.
relevance: Clinical decision support AI system with safety constraints and clinician-supervised design
key_findings: Superior effectiveness vs standard baselines in both simulated and clinical settings
Rule-based safety module blocks contraindicated treatments
Low latency with expert consultation needed for minority of cases
Continuous learning loop from practical use
tools_evaluated: Proposed CDSAS with Digital Twin + RL
scale: Synthetic clinical simulator + TCGA ovarian cancer dataset

title: Compositional Reasoning Depth Predicts Clinical AI Failure: Empirical Evidence Consistent with Transformer Compositionality Limits in EHR Question Answering
authors: Sanjay Basu
abstract: Introduces hop-count taxonomy as predictor of LLM failure on EHR QA. Questions requiring more inferential steps produce disproportionately more errors. All tested models show monotone accuracy decline with hop count. Extended thinking did not flatten accuracy-depth curve. Hop count is cross-architecture predictor of LLM error on EHR QA.
relevance: Clinical AI safety - predicts when clinical AI systems fail based on reasoning complexity, deployment risk stratification
key_findings: Monotone accuracy decline with hop count across all models (Claude, GPT-4o, GPT-5.4)
OR per hop: 0.72 (Claude), 0.58 (GPT-4o), 0.80 (GPT-5.4) - all statistically significant
Extended thinking did not significantly flatten accuracy-depth curve
Hop count is theory-motivated, cross-architecture predictor of clinical AI error
scale: 313 MedAlign EHR QA pairs, 4 hop levels, 3 models, 2 providers

title: The Critical Role of Model Selection in Causal Inference: InferBERT Framework for Pharmacovigilance
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Distinguishing causal adverse drug events (ADEs) from spurious correlations is central to pharmacovigilance. The InferBERT framework integrates transformer models with Do-calculus, but its success hinges on the underlying classification model. Comparative analysis evaluates the impact of model selection on causal accuracy in pharmacovigilance signal detection.
relevance: Relevant to clinical AI tool safety for medication-related decisions — pharmacovigilance is core to clinical decision support
key_findings: Model selection choice significantly impacts causal inference performance in InferBERT framework
Comparative analysis quantifies sensitivity of ADE signal detection to underlying transformer models
Do-calculus integration provides stronger theoretical grounding for clinical causal reasoning
Implications for clinical AI tools offering drug safety or interaction analysis
scale: Pharmacovigilance dataset (comprehensive comparison)

title: Medical Heuristic Learning: An LLM-Driven Framework for Interpretable and Auditable Clinical Decision Rules
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Predictive modeling for clinical decision support requires transparent decision logic. Although deep learning and tree ensemble methods achieve high accuracy, black-box nature remains a major obstacle to clinical deployment. This LLM-driven framework produces interpretable and auditable clinical decision rules directly from data, balancing transparency with performance.
relevance: Direct relevance to OpenEvidence's EvidenceGrade feature (Jul 10 launch) — interpretable clinical decision-making is core to physician trust
key_findings: LLM-driven framework produces interpretable clinical decision rules
Bridges the gap between high-accuracy black-box models and auditable clinical reasoning
Rules can be reviewed and audited by clinicians before deployment
Aligns with emerging medical AI transparency requirements (EU AI Act Aug 2026)
tools_evaluated: LLM-driven heuristic learning framework vs deep learning and tree ensemble baselines
scale: Multiple clinical decision support tasks

title: Prescribing Caution: A Critique of OpenEvidence to Answer Medication-Related Questions
authors: Bergsbaken JM et al.
abstract: Critique of OpenEvidence's accuracy answering medication-related clinical questions. Identifies specific gaps and areas for improvement in pharmacotherapy recommendations.
relevance: Direct evaluation of OpenEvidence on medication-related questions
key_findings: Identified gaps in OpenEvidence medication recommendations
scale: Medication-related clinical questions

title: Reproducibility of AI-Generated Antibiotic Recommendations in Standardized Clinical Scenarios
authors: De Vito A et al.
abstract: Evaluates reproducibility of AI-generated antibiotic recommendations across standardized clinical scenarios. Tests consistency and reliability of clinical AI recommendations.
relevance: Reproducibility evaluation — critical for clinical AI reliability assessment
key_findings: Tests reproducibility of AI antibiotic recommendations
scale: Standardized clinical scenarios

title: ClinHallu: A Benchmark for Diagnosing Stage-Wise Hallucinations in Medical MLLM Reasoning
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Building trustworthy medical multimodal large language models is critical for reliable clinical decision support. Existing medical hallucination benchmarks focus on data collection but ignore where hallucinations originate within reasoning. ClinHallu identifies stage-wise hallucinations in medical MLLM reasoning — pinpointing exactly where in the reasoning chain a hallucination emerges, enabling targeted mitigation strategies.
relevance: Direct benchmark for clinical AI safety — addresses hallucination origins in medical MLLM reasoning, complementary to NOHARM and HealthBench
key_findings: Identifies stage-wise hallucinations emerging at specific points in medical MLLM reasoning chains
More actionable than endpoint accuracy-only hallucination benchmarks
Enables targeted mitigation strategies at specific reasoning stages
Critical for clinical deployment where hallucination at any reasoning stage can produce harmful guidelines
scale: Multi-stage reasoning evaluation across medical MLLM benchmarks

title: A Computational Audit of Demographic Association Encoding in ClinicalBERT Language Predictions
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Transformer-based clinical language models are increasingly integrated into high-stakes clinical decision support pipelines, yet the computational mechanisms through which demographic associations encoded in medical documentation propagate into model probability distributions remain empirically underexplored. Provides a computational audit quantifying demographic bias propagation in ClinicalBERT.
relevance: Critical for clinical AI fairness — quantifies how demographic bias encoded in clinical documentation propagates into predictions made by widely used clinical NLP models (ClinicalBERT underpins many EHR-integrated AI deployments)
key_findings: Computational audit reveals demographic associations encoded in ClinicalBERT probability distributions
Quantifies demographic bias propagation from training documentation through to predictions
Identifies specific encoding pathways that can amplify or mitigate fairness issues
Implications for any clinical decision support tool built on ClinicalBERT-like clinical language models
scale: Computational audit of demographic encoding pathways

title: Can Post-Training Turn LLMs into Good Medical Coders? An Empirical Study of Generative ICD Coding
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Automated International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding is a core medical-coding task for billing, epidemiology, and clinical decision support. Generative LLMs are often reported as weak medical coders, but this finding comes mostly from inference-time settings. Empirical study investigates whether post-training (fine-tuning and instruction tuning) can substantially close the gap to specialist ICD coding systems.
relevance: Directly relevant to clinical AI workflow tool evaluations — ICD coding is a high-volume billing/clinical task where LLMs compete with OpenEvidence's Coding Intelligence module (launched Mar 2026)
key_findings: Empirical evaluation of post-training techniques for generative ICD coding
Compares inference-time LLM coding vs post-training-tuned coding models
Quantifies how much post-training closes the gap to specialist ICD coding systems
Implications for deploying generative LLMs in medical-coding pipelines
scale: ICD coding benchmark datasets

title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Five Large Language Models in Anesthesia Decision-Making
authors: Chen R et al.
abstract: Large-scale evaluation of 5 LLMs on anesthesia decision-making tasks. Assesses clinical reasoning and safety in perioperative scenarios.
relevance: Evaluation of LLMs in anesthesia — specialty-specific benchmarking
key_findings: 5 LLMs evaluated on anesthesia decision-making
scale: Anesthesia decision-making scenarios

title: Assessment of OpenEvidence responses to AAOS clinical practice guidelines for ACL reconstruction
authors: El Kayali MK et al.
abstract: Assesses OpenEvidence's responses against AAOS clinical practice guidelines for ACL reconstruction. Measures adherence to established orthopedic guidelines.
relevance: Direct evaluation of OpenEvidence against established clinical guidelines
key_findings: Assesses OpenEvidence adherence to AAOS guidelines
scale: ACL reconstruction guideline scenarios

title: Can AI Agents Synthesize Scientific Conclusions? SciConBench
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Scientific AI agents increasingly retrieve evidence, reason across sources, and synthesize conclusions used in consequential decisions. Yet their ability to do so in high-stakes domains such as health remains unclear. Introduces SciConBench, a large-scale live benchmark of 9.11K questions and experiments evaluating whether AI agents can synthesize scientific conclusions reliably in domains including health.
relevance: Directly relevant to clinical AI evaluation — tests whether RAG-based systems (OpenEvidence's core architecture) can synthesize scientific evidence reliably into conclusions used in health decisions
key_findings: SciConBench covers 9,110 questions across multiple scientific domains including health
Evaluates AI agents on evidence retrieval, cross-source reasoning, and conclusion synthesis
Tests whether AI conclusions are reliable in high-stakes health domains
Methodology relevant to evaluating any RAG-based clinical decision support system
tools_evaluated: Multiple AI agents + retrieval-augmented generation systems
scale: 9,110 scientific synthesis questions across domains

title: Beyond Prediction: Longitudinal Reasoning in EHR-Integrated Clinical AI
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Structured analysis of how contemporary clinical AI systems integrate electronic health record (EHR) data and the extent to which they support longitudinal clinical reasoning. Drawing on a curated corpus of clinical NLP and EHR-integrated systems, develops a framework for evaluating whether EHR-integrated clinical AI supports multi-visit longitudinal reasoning beyond single-prediction tasks.
relevance: Directly relevant to EHR-integrated clinical AI tools — OpenEvidence now deployed at Mount Sinai (Epic), Sutter, Cedars-Sinai, NYP (all Epic) where longitudinal reasoning quality affects clinical utility
key_findings: Develops framework for evaluating EHR-integrated clinical AI longitudinal reasoning capabilities
Curated corpus analysis of existing clinical NLP and EHR-integrated systems
Identifies gap between single-prediction tasks and true multi-visit longitudinal clinical reasoning
Implications for major EHR-embedded AI deployments including OpenEvidence
tools_evaluated: Curated corpus of clinical NLP and EHR-integrated clinical AI systems
scale: Multi-system structured analysis

title: When Large Language Models Fail in Healthcare: Evaluating Sensitivity to Prompt Variations
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in healthcare for clinical question answering, diagnosis support, and report summarization. Despite their promise, these models remain highly sensitive to subtle prompt perturbations, both lexical and syntactic, posing serious risks in clinical contexts where minor wording changes from a clinician could produce materially different recommendations.
relevance: Directly addresses safety of clinical AI tools where clinicians enter free-text queries — quantifies how minor prompt wording changes affect medical LLM outputs, complementing NOHARM and HealthBench safety benchmarks
key_findings: Quantifies sensitivity of medical LLMs to subtle lexical and syntactic prompt perturbations
Demonstrates that minor clinician-side wording changes can produce materially different clinical recommendations
Poses serious safety risks in clinical contexts where free-text queries are the norm
Implications for all clinical query-answering tools including OpenEvidence
tools_evaluated: Multiple LLMs in clinical question answering, diagnosis support, report summarization
scale: Prompt perturbation study across healthcare tasks

title: AI Rater Discrimination Depends on Scoring Protocol in Complex Clinical Decision-Making
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Clinical AI evaluation increasingly delegates scoring to large language models acting as AI raters, yet their scoring behavior across evaluation conditions has not been quantitatively characterized. Factorial study of AI rater behavior in adult type 2 diabetes clinical decision-making quantifies how different scoring protocols affect LLM rater discrimination between treatment options.
relevance: Methodologically relevant to all clinical AI benchmarks — evaluates whether LLM raters used to score clinical AI outputs are themselves reliable judges (relevant to NOHARM, HealthBench, MedQA scoring)
key_findings: Factorial study of AI rater behavior reveals scoring-protocol-dependent discrimination
Adult type 2 diabetes clinical decision-making is the worked example
Different scoring protocols produce materially different clinical AI quality assessments
Implications for benchmark validity when AI raters score clinical AI outputs
tools_evaluated: Multiple AI raters + varying scoring protocols
scale: Factorial evaluation design across clinical decision scenarios

title: ClinicalMC: A Benchmark for Multi-Course Clinical Decision-Making with Large Language Models
authors: Multiple authors
abstract: Large language models have been widely adopted in healthcare, yet they still encounter significant challenges in complex clinical decision-making scenarios. Existing benchmarks primarily assess LLM performance in single-course settings and lack systematic evaluation in multi-course scenarios. ClinicalMC introduces systematic multi-course clinical decision-making benchmark evaluation.
relevance: Direct clinical AI benchmark — addresses gap in multi-course (vs single-course) LLM clinical decision-making evaluation, complementary to NOHARM and HealthBench
key_findings: Introduces ClinicalMC benchmark for multi-course clinical decision-making
Addresses gap in existing benchmarks that assess only single-course scenarios
Systematic evaluation across complex clinical decision-making scenarios
Identifies specific failure modes of LLMs in multi-course clinical reasoning
tools_evaluated: Multiple LLMs in multi-course clinical decision-making
scale: Multi-course clinical decision scenarios (LLM evaluation benchmark)

title: The Reliability Gap in Benchmark Auditing: Distribution Shift and Scale as Failure Modes of Contamination Detection
authors: Wojciech Zarzecki, Jan Dubiński, Sebastian Cygert
abstract: Identifies two understudied failure modes in benchmark contamination detection — distribution shift (where suspect and validation sets violate the IID assumption) and scale constraints (large realistic auditing scenarios vs small controlled academic regimes). Concerns the validity of LLM benchmark auditing in clinical AI (NOHARM, HealthBench, MedQA, USMLE, MedCheck) where training-data contamination detection is critical to scoring integrity.
relevance: Reveals failure modes in LLM benchmark contamination detection that affect scoring validity for clinical AI benchmarks (NOHARM, HealthBench, MedQA)
key_findings: Two understudied contamination-detection failure modes: distribution shift + scale constraints
Standard statistical tools validated only in controlled academic regimes (large, homogeneous corpora)
Realistic clinical AI auditing scenarios violate the IID assumption
Has implications for NOHARM, HealthBench, MedQA scoring integrity
scale: Methodological failure-mode analysis

title: Integrating AI into infection control: Evaluating the accuracy and consistency of four leading platforms across three regions
authors: Julkipli J et al.
abstract: Evaluates accuracy and consistency of 4 leading AI platforms across 3 regions for infection control questions.
journal: J Assoc Med Microbiol Infect Dis Can
relevance: Cross-regional evaluation of clinical AI platforms in infectious disease
key_findings: 4 platforms evaluated across 3 geographic regions
scale: Infection control scenarios, 3 regions

title: Evaluation of Clinically-Focused Artificial Intelligence Chatbots for Answering Drug Information Questions
authors: Ipema H, Munir F, Sarna K, Wasynczuk J, Saiyad Z
abstract: Comparative study of four clinically focused AI chatbots (OpenEvidence, Clair, GlassHealth, DougallGPT) and one general-purpose chatbot (ChatGPT) answering 30 drug information questions previously answered by drug-information pharmacists; scored by three pharmacy faculty using the 25-point CLEAR framework (Completeness, Lack of false info, Evidence, Appropriateness, Relevance). OpenEvidence had the highest mean total CLEAR score (17.82/25), followed by ChatGPT (15.72/25); both categorized as "average" content. None produced a majority of "very good" responses (19-25 points). All AI chatbots scored statistically lower than faculty responses. Pharmacist expertise remains essential for drug-information answers.
relevance: Direct head-to-head: OpenEvidence vs three other clinically focused AI chatbots plus ChatGPT on pharmacy drug-information questions; OpenEvidence highest-scoring
key_findings: OpenEvidence total CLEAR 17.82/25 ("average" tier) — highest of 5 AI chatbots tested
ChatGPT 15.72/25 ("average"); closely matched OpenEvidence overall
Clair, GlassHealth, DougallGPT scores below ChatGPT
All AI chatbots statistically lower than pharmacy faculty responses
Lack of false information had highest sub-score across AIs; evidence supporting content had lowest
Few responses from any chatbot rated "very good" (19-25 CLEAR points)
Authors: pharmacist expertise remains essential for drug-information answers
scale: 30 drug-information questions; evaluation by 3 pharmacy faculty; CLEAR framework (25 points)

title: Arkangel AI, OpenEvidence, ChatGPT, Medisearch: Are They Objectively up to Medical Standards? A Real-Life Assessment of LLM Chatbots in Health Care
authors: Castaño-Villegas N, Villa MC, Barrientos KM, Llano I, Velásquez L, Zea J
abstract: Independent (Arkangel AI) comparative study of four LLM chatbots (Arkangel AI, OpenEvidence, ChatGPT, Medisearch) on four clinical vignettes (orthopedics, pediatrics, gynecology, psychiatry) with four questions each (diagnosis, clinical management, research, general knowledge); evaluated by external clinicians on 8-criterion Likert scale. Response times recorded. Real-world assessment explicitly comparing consumer-facing and clinical chatbots side-by-side.
relevance: Independent four-way comparison including OpenEvidence on standardized clinical vignettes in four specialties; adds to head-to-head coverage beyond US-centric NOHARM/Real-POCQi studies

title: Large Language Model Hallucinations in Spine Surgery: A Comparative Analysis of Clinician vs Patient-Level Prompts
authors: McLaughlin ND, Srinivas AN, Lowe ZF, Botterbush KS, Patel MS, Avila MJ
abstract: Evaluates fabricated citations ("hallucinations") produced by five LLMs — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, OpenEvidence — on common neurosurgical spine topics; explicitly compares clinician vs patient-level prompts. Quantifies citation accuracy across systems and identifies which prompts are riskier for misinformation. Adds OpenEvidence to a growing list of multi-system spine/neurosurgery comparisons and tests whether physician framing reduces hallucination risk.

Quantifies fabricated citations ("hallucinations") on common neurosurgical spine topics

title: ChatHealthAI: Aligning Electronic Health Record Representations with Large Language Models for Grounded Clinical Reasoning
authors: Bo-Hong Wang, Baicheng Peng, Ruilin Wang, Jun Bai, Ziyang Song
abstract: Proposes ChatHealthAI — a multimodal reasoning framework that aligns structured EHR representations from a pretrained EHR foundation model with the semantic space of a frozen LLM through a task-aware resampler. Integrates longitudinal patient data into grounded clinical reasoning. Designed to bridge the gap between EHR foundation models (predictive but opaque) and LLMs (interpretable but weak on structured EHR data). Directly applicable to clinical decision support tools that integrate patient chart data.
relevance: Multimodal framework combining structured EHR foundation model representations with LLM semantic space for grounded clinical reasoning; advances integration of patient chart data into clinical AI

Integrates longitudinal patient data into grounded clinical reasoning
Bridges EHR foundation models (predictive but opaque) with LLMs (interpretable but weak on structured data)
Directly relevant to EHR-integrated clinical decision support

title: Med-HEAL: Analyzing and Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical LLMs with Hallucination-Aware In-Context Learning
authors: Yiming Liao, Zeno Franco, Jose Eduardo Lizarraga Mazaba
abstract: Hallucinations in medical LLMs pose risks for clinical decision support, especially over complex EHRs. Existing benchmarks lack realistic clinical context and offer limited mitigation insight. Introduces Med-HEAL framework for systematically identifying and mitigating hallucinations via hallucination-aware in-context learning grounded in real clinical workflows.
relevance: Specifically targets hallucination risk in EHR-grounded medical LLM reasoning — directly applicable to safety case for clinical AI tools like OpenEvidence
key_findings: Formalizes hallucination detection at process level within clinical contexts
Demonstrates hallucination-aware in-context learning reduces critical errors in EHR-grounded reasoning
Provides reproducible benchmark for hallucination evaluation in realistic clinical workflows
Mitigation technique compatible with retrieval-augmented clinical AI assistants

title: Utility of the Medical Knowledge AI Copilot, OpenEvidence: A Patient With 100 Cerebral Microhemorrhages
authors: Navarra AN, Ikramuddin S, Greenberg SM, Doraiswamy PM
abstract: Duke clinical case report illustrating the real-world utility of OpenEvidence in managing a diagnostically complex presentation — a patient with approximately 100 cerebral microhemorrhages (consistent with probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy). Authors describe how OpenEvidence's sourced, cited answers informed differential diagnosis and management discussion. Adds to growing literature of curated clinical case reports documenting OpenEvidence clinical utility.
relevance: Illustrative Duke case report of OpenEvidence use in diagnostic workup of a patient with 100 cerebral microhemorrhages (probable CAA)

title: Can LLMs Score Medical Diagnoses and Clinical Reasoning as well as Expert Panels?
authors: Amy Rouillard et al.
abstract: Evaluating medical AI systems using expert clinician panels is costly and slow, motivating the use of LLMs as alternative adjudicators. We evaluate an LLM jury composed of three frontier AI models scoring 3,333 diagnoses on 300 real-world middle-income country (MIC) hospital cases. Results provide compelling evidence that a calibrated, multi-model LLM jury can serve as a trustworthy and reliable proxy for expert clinician evaluation in medical AI benchmarking.
relevance: Validates LLM jury approach as proxy for expert clinician evaluation in medical AI benchmarking — important for scaling benchmark evaluations
key_findings: Calibrated multi-model LLM jury can serve as trustworthy proxy for expert clinician evaluation
3,333 diagnoses scored on 300 real-world MIC hospital cases
Compelling evidence for reliability of LLM-based evaluation in medical AI

title: Towards Reliable Medical LLMs: Benchmarking and Enhancing Confidence Estimation in Medical Consultation
authors: Zhiyao Ren et al.
abstract: Evaluates confidence estimation in LLMs during clinical consultations. Existing benchmarks evaluate single-turn static settings; this study addresses multi-turn evidence accumulation. Finds significant gaps in model confidence calibration.

Models show poor confidence calibration as evidence accumulates
Proposes methods for enhancing confidence estimation

title: The accuracy and repeatability of OpenEvidence on complex medical subspecialty scenarios: a pilot study
authors: Jagarapu J, Babata K, Chamarthi S, Hoyt R
abstract: OpenEvidence scored 100% on USMLE-type multiple-choice questions, but has not been tested on more complex medical scenarios. This study tested OE and Deep Consult (DC) models using questions from the MedXpertQA dataset comprising 100 medical subspecialty scenarios with two independent evaluators. The highest accuracy for DC was 41%, and for OE, 34%. Repeatability testing revealed evaluator concordance of 77% for OE and 72% for DC. Results indicate OE is suitable for straightforward guideline lookups but struggles with complex multi-step reasoning.
relevance: Direct evaluation of OpenEvidence accuracy and repeatability on complex subspecialty scenarios — reveals significant limitations vs USMLE performance
key_findings: Deep Consult max accuracy: 41% on MedXpertQA subspecialty scenarios
Quick Consult max accuracy: 34% on same dataset
Repeatability: 77% concordance for OE, 72% for DC between two evaluators
No statistically significant difference between OE and DC accuracy (p=0.09)
DC provides ~6.7x more references than OE (34.7 vs 5.2 average) but accuracy gain not significant
Treatment tasks had highest accuracy (OE: 43.9%, DC: 47%); Basic science lowest (OE: 23.5%, DC: 32.4%)
75% of the time OE and DC were discordant on the same question
Conclusion: OE suitable for straightforward guideline lookups, not complex multi-step reasoning

title: NOHARM (Numerous Options Harm Assessment for Risk in Medicine): A medical safety benchmark and randomized study of physician and AI teaming on clinical consultations
authors: David Wu, Fateme Nateghi Haredasht, Ethan Goh, Adam Rodman, Jonathan H. Chen, et al.
abstract: 1,100-task benchmark of primary care-to-specialist consultation cases measuring harmful errors from LLM-generated medical consultation recommendations. Covers 10 specialties, 12,747 expert annotations, 4,249 clinical management options. Tests 20 LLMs and 4 RAG clinical AI tools. Direct application carried potential for severe harm in up to 24.6% of cases. Errors of omission >80% of severe errors. Multi-agent AI teaming improved performance. Randomized study of 101 U.S.-licensed physicians showed AI assistance improved performance vs conventional resources, but AI-assisted physicians frequently omitted valuable AI recommendations.
relevance: Directly evaluates OpenEvidence and 3 other RAG clinical AI tools for clinical harm potential
key_findings: Stanford-Harvard ARISE free-choice arm revealed preference: physicians chose OpenEvidence in 22.3% of cases — more than ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and all other external AI combined (19.8%)
24.6% of cases carried potential for severe harm from AI recommendations
Errors of omission accounted for >80% of severe errors
Clinical AI tools outperformed generalist LLMs
Multi-agent AI teaming further improved performance
AI-assisted physicians improved vs conventional resources
Combined human-AI responses would outperform both alone if AI recommendations were fully incorporated
scale: 1,100 tasks, 10 specialties, 12,747 annotations, 4,249 options, 101 physicians

title: Generalist Large Language Models Outperform Clinical Tools on Medical Benchmarks
authors: Karthik Vishwanath et al.
abstract: Independent evaluation of two clinical AI tools (OpenEvidence and UpToDate Expert AI) against three frontier LLMs (GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5) using 1,000-item benchmark (MedQA + HealthBench). Generalist models consistently outperformed clinical tools. Published in Nature Medicine.

key_findings: GPT-5 achieved highest scores across all stages
OpenEvidence and UpToDate showed deficits in completeness, communication quality, context awareness, and safety reasoning
Frontier LLMs outperformed specialized clinical tools on medical knowledge and clinician alignment

title: Beyond the Leaderboard: Rethinking Medical Benchmarks for Large Language Models (MedCheck)
authors: Wenxuan Wang et al.
abstract: Meta-evaluation of 56 medical LLM benchmarks using the MedCheck framework. Finds widespread systemic issues: disconnect from clinical practice, data integrity crises from contamination, and systematic neglect of safety-critical evaluation dimensions like model robustness and uncertainty awareness.

title: A Novel Evaluation Benchmark for Medical LLMs: Illuminating Safety and Effectiveness in Clinical Domains (CSEDB)
authors: Multiple
abstract: Clinical Safety-Effectiveness Dual-Track Benchmark (CSEDB) — 30-criteria framework built on clinical expert consensus. 2,069 open-ended Q&A items across 26 clinical departments. Tested 6 LLMs: moderate overall performance (57.2%), safety 54.7%, effectiveness 62.3%. 13.3% performance drop in high-risk scenarios. Domain-specific medical LLMs outperformed general-purpose models.

Safety scores (54.7%) lower than effectiveness (62.3%)
13.3% performance drop in high-risk scenarios

title: AI-based Clinical Decision Support for Primary Care: A Real-World Study
authors: Multiple (Penda Health team)
abstract: Real-world study of an LLM-based clinical decision support tool (AI Consult) at Penda Health clinics in Nairobi, Kenya. The system triggers asynchronously during clinical workflow decision points in the EMR. AI group clinicians saw significant reductions in clinical failure modes including incorrect primary diagnosis, inappropriate medications, missing patient education and follow-up plans, and missing history/investigation details. LLM evaluators found greater differences than physician evaluators (22% reduction in treatment errors, 19% in diagnostic errors).

LLM evaluators found 22% reduction in treatment errors, 19% in diagnostic errors
Effect became more pronounced after active clinician uptake strategies

authors: Multiple

key_findings: 2,996 questions from real EHRs and clinical scenarios
Automated LLM-as-Judge pipeline validated against expert scoring

title: Grounded in Consensus, In Step With Emerging Science: A Consensus-Anchored Multi-Corpus Clinical Chatbot for Long COVID
authors: Yining Wu, Philip DiGiacomo, Ying Ding, William Brode
abstract: Long COVID poses a challenge for clinical decision support because relevant evidence is distributed across sources with different update cycles, evidentiary roles, and levels of clinical maturity. The authors present a clinician-facing chatbot that organizes four sources within a retrieval-augmented workflow: expert-curated consensus guidance, current PubMed literature, registered interventional trials, and evidence from living systematic reviews. Consensus guidance is always included to frame responses, while the remaining sources are retrieved in parallel when selected by the user. In an exploratory automated evaluation on 50 clinician-facing questions, the chatbot showed comparable mean ratings to OpenEvidence, with numerically higher scores and lower score variability in an LLM-judged comparison.
relevance: Directly compares a new RAG-based clinical chatbot against OpenEvidence on 50 clinician-facing questions, demonstrating comparable performance with lower score variability
key_findings: Presents a consensus-anchored multi-corpus RAG chatbot for Long COVID clinical decision support
Organizes four evidence sources: consensus guidance, PubMed literature, clinical trials, and living systematic reviews
Shows comparable mean ratings to OpenEvidence on 50 clinician-facing questions with numerically higher scores and lower score variability
Demonstrates that consensus-anchored retrieval can match or exceed specialized clinical AI tools on specific clinical domains

title: Aletheia: An Offline-First Clinical Decision Support System for Differential Diagnosis in Low-Resource Healthcare Settings
authors: Joseph Walusimbi, Ann Move Oguti, Abubakhari Sserwadda, Precious Boss Kasasira, Charles Brian Okoboi
abstract: Access to specialist clinical expertise remains severely limited across sub-Saharan Africa, where physician-to-patient ratios can fall below 1:25,000 in rural settings. Existing AI-assisted diagnostic tools predominantly require reliable internet connectivity and high-specification hardware, rendering them impractical for frontline healthcare workers in district hospitals and health centres. This paper presents Aletheia, an offline-first clinical decision support system designed for low-resource healthcare contexts across sub-Saharan Africa. Aletheia is built upon Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, fine-tuned using Quantised Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) on a curated dataset of 27,000 clinical reasoning samples spanning 50 disease conditions with elevated prevalence in East Africa. Evaluation demonstrates a Top-1 diagnostic accuracy of 80.0%, Top-3 accuracy of 100.0%, BERTScore-F1 of 0.909, and METEOR of 0.467 across ten representative clinical case categories. The system achieves an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.275 and passes the Africa Deep Tech Challenge 2026 memory budget constraint of 7,168 MB, achieving a peak inference RAM of approximately 3,630 MB.
relevance: Presents a novel offline-first clinical decision support system using fine-tuned LLM for differential diagnosis, demonstrating feasibility of deployable clinical AI in resource-constrained settings without cloud infrastructure
key_findings: Offline-first CDSS using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with QLoRA fine-tuning on 27,000 clinical reasoning samples
Top-1 diagnostic accuracy of 80.0% and Top-3 accuracy of 100.0% across 50 disease conditions
Peak inference RAM of ~3,630 MB, meeting the ADTC 2026 memory budget constraint
Demonstrates feasibility of LLM-based clinical reasoning at primary care level without cloud infrastructure
scale: 27,000 training samples; 50 disease conditions; 10 representative clinical case categories

title: Retrieval, not hallucinations, will be the limiting factor for LLM-based clinical AI tools
authors: Kirk Roberts, Steven Bedrick, Kurt Miller, William R. Hersh, Hongfang Liu
abstract: Discussions around large language model (LLM) errors in clinical artificial intelligence (AI) generally center around precision errors like hallucinations. This perspective, targeting both clinicians and AI researchers, seeks to shift that discussion to recall errors, particularly in retrieval of patient-level data needed for many clinical AI tools. The perspective outlines types of errors and mitigation strategies, describes research directions in LLMs and retrieval, and provides an overview of retrieval evaluation.
relevance: Shifts focus from hallucination (precision) to retrieval (recall) as the key limiting factor for LLM-based clinical AI tools, directly relevant to RAG-based systems like OpenEvidence
key_findings: Argues that recall errors in retrieval of patient-level data, not hallucinations, will be the primary limiting factor for clinical AI tools
Outlines types of retrieval errors and mitigation strategies for LLM-based clinical AI
Describes research directions in LLMs and retrieval for clinical applications
Provides overview of retrieval evaluation methodologies relevant to RAG-based clinical decision support
scale: Perspective/review

title: Performance of 5 Large Language Models in Perioperative Consultation for Pediatric Hypospadias: Cross-Sectional Comparative Study
authors: Kang T, Yuan C, Hu X, Huang W
abstract: Cross-sectional comparison of 5 LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, OpenEvidence, Zhipu Qingyan, DeepSeek) on 10 pediatric hypospadias perioperative questions. Evaluated by 23 pediatric urology experts (6 dimensions) and 36 caregivers (4 dimensions). Gemini-2.5-Pro ranked first (expert median 5.0; caregiver 4.0). DeepSeek second with superior Empathy vs ChatGPT-4o (r=-0.343; P<.001). OpenEvidence scored lowest (2.0 both), despite 100% verifiable citation accuracy (vs DeepSeek 33% fabricated, Zhipu Qingyan 24%). 8-reviewer clinical safety audit: 78 flags including 9 Severe-level flags across 5 question-model combinations; OpenEvidence carried the largest Severe burden (5 of 9) and the highest severity-weighted score — direct head-to-head test where OE citation integrity coexists with clinical-safety gap.
relevance: High — OpenEvidence is one of 5 LLMs compared head-to-head; finds OE has 100% citation accuracy but lowest overall ranking and highest severe-safety burden on a surgical subspecialty topic
key_findings: OpenEvidence scored lowest overall ranking (median 2.0/5 from both experts and caregivers)
OpenEvidence citation accuracy was 100% verifiable (F=0%) — strongest of all five models
OpenEvidence carried 5 of 9 Severe-level safety flags (the largest severe burden of any model tested)
Citation accuracy and clinical safety were dissociable — fully verifiable references did not protect from harm
Gemini-2.5-Pro ranked first; DeepSeek second; ChatGPT-4o, OE, Zhipu Qingyan clustered lower
Expert-caregiver agreement was strong (Spearman ρ=0.89; P=.04)
scale: 10 high-priority caregiver-selected questions; 23 expert + 36 caregiver evaluators; 8-reviewer clinical safety audit

title: Artificial Intelligence Use in Clinical Reasoning Among Second-Year Medical Students: A Cross-Sectional Survey Study
authors: Redhage D, Allen W, Schuknecht A, Mortinsen R
abstract: Survey of 28 second-year medical students at USD Sanford SOM on AI use in clinical reasoning. ChatGPT most-used (~90%), followed by OpenEvidence. Most frequent uses: suggesting diagnostic tests, proposing management strategies, and clarifying medical knowledge — indicating early integration into clinical reasoning workflows. Concerns: overreliance on AI, loss of independent diagnostic reasoning, and incorrect AI-generated information.
relevance: Medium — Captures trainee adoption; OpenEvidence is the second most-cited platform after ChatGPT among pre-clinical medical students, complementing the physician-level adoption metrics
key_findings: ChatGPT most-used (~90%) among second-year medical students, followed by OpenEvidence
Most-frequent uses: diagnostic test suggestions, management strategies, knowledge clarification
Identified concerns: overreliance, loss of independent diagnostic reasoning, inaccurate outputs
