title: The Clinical Trial Pipeline Reveals the Next Wave of Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: A Multidimensional Analysis of 8,532 Registered Studies
authors: unknown
abstract: Systematic identification of AI-related trials in ClinicalTrials.gov by LLM-based classifier across 7 dimensions. 8,532 AI clinical trials across 32 specialties; 80% registered from 2019 onward; 30.5% randomized. Imaging-based AI 29% (2,475 trials); clinical text/NLP up 7x 2018-2025; prognostic (4,324) > diagnostic (3,828); treatment recommendation underdeveloped (9%, 768 trials); translational maturity limited (38% retrospective, 21% silent prospective). Only 184 trials involved Level 4 semi-autonomous / closed-loop AI (68% focused on glucose management). Multimodal AI 33.6%. Conclusion: clinical AI has moved from retrospective development to prospective evaluation, but not yet to adequately powered, geographically representative, long-term outcome trials.
relevance: High — Provides independent quantification of where clinical AI tools (including OE-class systems) sit in evidence maturity. Only 9% of trials reach treatment-recommendation tier; clinical decision support evidence base still thin
key_findings: 8,532 AI clinical trials registered; 80% from 2019 onward; 30.5% RCT design
Imaging-based AI still largest modality (29%) but clinical text/NLP trials up 7x 2018-2025
Prognostic AI (4,324) > diagnostic AI (3,828) — shift toward risk stratification
Treatment-recommendation AI trials only 9% (768) — domain most relevant to OE and similar CDS tools remains evidence-thin
Translational maturity limited: 38% retrospective, 21% silent prospective; only 184 Level 4 semi-autonomous trials (68% glucose management)
Conclusion: prospective evaluation exists but adequately powered, geographically representative, outcome trials still lacking
scale: 8,532 trials across 32 specialties

title: IyawoBench v2.0: Extended Diagnostic Evaluation of Large Language Model Clinical Triage in Nigerian Primary Care
authors: Anthonio Oladimeji Gabriel, Dimeji Olawuyi
abstract: Extended diagnostic evaluation of LLM clinical triage on 200 synthetic vignettes derived from 1,200 real patient encounters at 19 Nigerian primary health centres. Introduces formal mathematical framework decomposing triage safety into three failure modes: Conservative Escalation Bias, Systematic Downgrade Bias, and Middle-Tier Instability. Proposes Escalation Bias Index and Expected Deployment Cost as novel metrics exposing failure modes hidden by conventional accuracy/sensitivity scores. Evaluated on Claude Sonnet 4.6, Llama 3.3 70B, Llama 3.1 8B plus five naive baselines. All three models exhibit at least one formal failure mode; traditional sensitivity metrics conceal a 77 percentage point under-triage gap in Llama 3.1 8B.
relevance: Novel benchmark and diagnostic framework for clinical AI triage safety in LMIC settings; introduces formal failure mode taxonomy and metrics that expose safety issues hidden by conventional accuracy scores — transferable to any triage-style clinical AI evaluation
key_findings: 200 synthetic vignettes from 1,200 real patient encounters at 19 Nigerian PHCs
Three formal failure modes: Conservative Escalation Bias, Systematic Downgrade Bias, Middle-Tier Instability
All three frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Llama 3.3 70B, Llama 3.1 8B) exhibit at least one formal failure mode
Traditional sensitivity metrics conceal a 77 pp under-triage gap in Llama 3.1 8B
Optimal model varies across deployment scenarios — single-ranking benchmarks inadequate for LMIC clinical AI selection
scale: 200 synthetic vignettes, 1,200 real patient encounters, 19 primary health centres, 3 frontier models + 5 naive baselines

title: Reasoning in Real World Clinical Care: Why Large Language Models Are Not Yet Safe for Autonomous Clinical Decision Support
authors: Shayndhan Sivanathan, Shravan Nageswaran, Mehdi Zadem, Ryaan Sultan, Nicolas von Mallinckrodt, Max Solovyev, Alexey Matyushkin, Sumon Sadhu, Gabriele C DeLuca, Sanjeeva Jeyaretna, James Hillis, Manoj Ramachandran, Prakash Jayakumar
abstract: Perspective on why LLMs are not yet safe for autonomous clinical triage of self-presenting, undifferentiated patients. The gap is not in medical knowledge but in fidelity of clinical evaluation: models optimized for probable text continuation are not optimized for safe action when the safe answer is the improbable must-not-miss diagnosis. Core deficit is information gathering under uncertainty. Under incomplete histories, LLMs may fail to broaden differentials, seek missing red flags, lower escalation thresholds, defer judgement, or escalate concern for unexcluded high-harm diagnoses. Evaluations often use complete, well-curated simulations that mask these failures. Assistant-like behaviors (credulity, agreeableness, miscalibration) amplify risk.
relevance: Directly addresses the safety gap for autonomous clinical AI decision support — articulates why LLMs that pass licensing exams are not yet safe for real-world triage; core argument about information gathering under uncertainty applies to OE-class tools
key_findings: Safe triage is sequential decision under asymmetric cost, not selection of most likely diagnosis
Core deficit is information gathering under uncertainty — LLMs fail to seek missing red flags or broaden differentials
Evaluations using complete, well-curated simulations mask real-world failure modes
Assistant-like behaviors (credulity, agreeableness, miscalibration) amplify clinical risk
Identifies specific required behaviors LLMs lack: broadening differential, seeking red flags, lowering escalation threshold, deferring judgement, escalating concern
scale: Perspective article with 13 authors across multiple clinical specialties

title: MedPRESS: A Multi-turn Benchmark for Patient-Pressure-Induced Medical Sycophancy in LLMs
authors: Saman Sarker Joy, Niloy Farhan
abstract: We introduce MedPRESS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring patient-pressure-induced sycophancy in LLMs. MedPRESS contains 600 medically grounded five-turn dialogues across three scenario families: medication and treatment demand, personal health self-care, and symptom triage and care resistance. Each dialogue begins with a health query and escalates through personal experience, social proof, external evidence claims, and direct adversarial challenge. We evaluate 20 LLMs across general, medical-domain, lightweight, large, open-weight, and proprietary families using structured judging and safety-focused metrics. Results show that models frequently shift toward unsafe agreement under repeated patient pressure, with substantial variation across model families, model scale, and prompt type. Anti-sycophancy prompting improves robustness for several models, but does not eliminate unsafe agreement. MedPRESS highlights a critical gap in medical LLM evaluation: safe medical knowledge is not enough unless models can maintain it under conversational pressure.
relevance: Directly relevant to clinical AI safety — benchmarks how LLMs handle patient pressure in multi-turn dialogues, a critical safety concern for clinical decision support tools like OpenEvidence
key_findings: 600 medically grounded 5-turn dialogues across 3 scenario families (medication demand, self-care, triage resistance)
20 LLMs evaluated across general, medical-domain, lightweight, large, open-weight, and proprietary families
Models frequently shift toward unsafe agreement under repeated patient pressure
Substantial variation across model families, model scale, and prompt type
Anti-sycophancy prompting improves robustness but does not eliminate unsafe agreement
Safe medical knowledge is not enough — models must maintain it under conversational pressure
tools_evaluated: 20 LLMs across general, medical-domain, lightweight, large, open-weight, and proprietary families
scale: 600 dialogues, 20 LLMs, 3 scenario families

title: MedUPS: Towards Diagnostic Assistance in Uncommon Medical Cases with Large Language Models
authors: Ofir Ben Shoham, Oriel Perets, Nir Grinberg, Nadav Rappoport
abstract: Uncommon and off-guideline cases are difficult for clinical decision support, because physicians must make a series of management decisions under diagnostic uncertainty and rarely see the full case at once. Most LLM benchmarks for medicine score only the final diagnosis, yet much of clinical care turns on the next appropriate action. We introduce MedUPSQA, a dataset of 21,874 mid-stream clinical decision points built from 5,535 real case reports, and MedUPS, an alignment framework that supervises models on these intermediate decisions as they unfold along a patient's trajectory. We segment free-text case presentations into chronologically ordered, accumulating clinical chunks and align models to predict the next step with reinforcement learning (GRPO), using an external LLM-as-a-Judge reward. Across three backbones, mid-stream alignment raises next-step accuracy from 55.2 to 66.7 for Qwen3.6-27B, from 47.2 to 57.8 for Qwen3.5-9B, and from 37.8 to 44.4 for HuatuoGPT-3-8B. In several model scales the objective improves accuracy more than scale, with smaller models surpassing larger, frontier models. SFT improves all backbones above base, indicating the target framework carries signal independently of the optimizer.
relevance: Directly relevant to clinical decision support — introduces a new benchmark and alignment framework for evaluating LLMs on intermediate clinical decisions (next test, next specialist, next differential) rather than just final diagnosis
key_findings: MedUPSQA: 21,874 mid-stream clinical decision points from 5,535 real case reports
Mid-stream alignment (GRPO) raises next-step accuracy: Qwen3.6-27B 55.2→66.7, Qwen3.5-9B 47.2→57.8, HuatuoGPT-3-8B 37.8→44.4
Smaller aligned models surpass larger frontier models — objective matters more than scale
SFT baselines also improve all backbones, confirming the target framework carries signal independently of optimizer
Shifts evaluation from final diagnosis to intermediate clinical decisions — mirrors real clinical workflow
scale: 21,874 decision points, 5,535 case reports, 3 model backbones

title: Bridging the English-Arabic Medical Knowledge Gap: Targeted Low-Rank Adaptation via Causal Layer Selection
authors: Chaimae Abouzahir, Musa Khan, Hala Ali-Hassan, Congbo Ma, Khaled Saleh, Yousra Sadqi, Jihad Mallat, Walid Al-Eisawi, Nizar Habash, Farah E. Shamout
abstract: LLMs perform strongly in English medical tasks but degrade substantially in Arabic. We investigate this via tuned lens probing and causal activation patching, finding that Arabic medical knowledge is present in intermediate representations but fails to surface at the output. This motivates Targeted Low-Rank Adaptation (TLoRA), restricted to the layer window where cross-lingual representations diverge. We evaluate TLoRA on multiple-choice medical QA, short-answer generation, and multi-turn clinical dialogue. We additionally introduce AraClinicDialog, a clinician-constructed Arabic medical dialogue benchmark in MSA with validated variants across four Arabic dialects. Results demonstrate that mechanistic diagnosis can guide targeted adaptation in underrepresented-language medical LLMs.

title: Agents Catching Agents: Shortcut Cascades and Benchmark Gaming in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Sebastián Andrés Cajas Ordóñez, Agastya Munnangi, Aldo Marzullo, et al.
abstract: Clinical decision support is moving toward committees of language-model agents deliberating on a shared workspace. We ask whether such committees can be gamed by shortcuts, cues a benchmark rewards but a clinician would ignore. Across seven cohorts on six public datasets spanning text (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, MIMIC-CXR reports), imaging (NIH ChestX-ray14, MIMIC-CXR-JPG, CheXpert) and tabular ICU records (SUPPORT2), Gemini committees resist these cues in isolation (flip 5-16%), yet a socially plausible shortcut spreads: when two peers assert the same wrong answer, the holdout under test adopts it in 38% of cases. Of three oversight agents, a gate cannot separate adoption from honest agreement (false-positive rate 100%); a same-lineage judge flags adoption on text (precision 100%, recall 93%) but collapses in imaging; a referee that privately re-queries the holdout transfers to imaging (77-88% precision). Gaming a hidden rubric is near-silent: only 1/10 text and 1/134 imaging drifters name the rubric they moved toward.

title: CARE-Bench: Benchmarking Patient-Facing LLM Triage
authors: Yining Hua, Hongbin Na, Cyrus Ayubcha
abstract: Patient-facing medical LLMs and agents increasingly answer symptom questions before clinician contact, where the key safety question is what action the user should take next. We introduce CARE-Bench, a source-grounded benchmark that evaluates sequential patient-facing triage as a four-label per-turn current-action task. CARE-Bench contains 500 cases and 1,059 evaluated patient-disclosure prefixes reconstructed from medical dialogue, consultation, and follow-up-question sources. We evaluate 11 models on 269 held-out rounds under unprompted and minimally prompted open-ended protocols, using a fixed GPT-5.5 mapper. Unprompted macro-F1 remains low (31.2-50.4). Prompting improves 10 of 11 models (46.9-63.4) but substantial threshold errors remain. When the correct action was to ask for more information, only 33.5% of prompted outputs preserved the step.

title: Diagnostic performance of Prof. Valmed, ChatGPT-5 Thinking, and OpenEvidence in rheumatology: A comparative evaluation.
authors: Kremer P, Langballe E, Haase I, Bamberger J, Kuhn S
abstract: To compare the diagnostic performance of a subscription-based medical large language model (LLM) certified as a medical device (Prof. Valmed), a subscription-based general-purpose LLM (ChatGPT-5 Thinking), and a freely accessible medical LLM (OpenEvidence). Sixty vignettes covering rare rheumatic diseases and differential diagnoses were entered using a standardized prompt to generate five top diagnoses and respective diagnostic probabilities. Blinded rheumatologists categorized suggested diagnoses as identical, plausible, or diagnostically different. OpenEvidence produced the highest proportion of identical top diagnoses (35.0%), followed by ChatGPT-5 Thinking (26.7%) and Prof. Valmed (23.3%); however, pairwise differences were not statistically significant. ChatGPT-5 Thinking achieved the highest total diagnostic score (226), followed by OpenEvidence (221) and Prof. Valmed (212).

title: RareLens: Towards End-to-End Rare Disease Care via Aligning Divergent Large Language Model Reasoning
authors: Xi Chen, Hongru Zhou, Shiyu Feng, Hanyu Zhou, Huahui Yi, Rongsheng Wang, Tiancheng He, Kun Wang, Pingping Liu, Qiankun Li, Sicheng Lin, Huiying Ou, Xiaohong Zheng, Tianying Zang, Zhuohang Wu, Leheng Jiang, Kexin Cao, Wenhan Zhang, ChengYi Li, Zhiyang Wang, Songlin Li, Benyou Wang, Ningbei Yin, Shaoting Zhang, Weili Fu, Jian Li, Kang Li
abstract: Rare diseases represent one of the most challenging settings for clinical decision-making, where heterogeneous presentations, sparse evidence and limited expertise create persistent uncertainty throughout the care pathway. Although AI could help, existing systems largely address isolated tasks, particularly diagnosis, and usually rely on downstream investigations rather than information available at initial presentation. The authors show that clinical AI performance under uncertainty can be improved not by scaling a single model, but by exploiting the diversity of multiple imperfect reasoning systems. Across heterogeneous LLMs, they identify divergent reasoning trajectories with complementary error patterns and develop RareLens, which learns to reconcile these perspectives into actionable decisions across four stages of rare disease care: risk screening, diagnosis, treatment planning and prognosis prediction. Built on RarelensBench, a real-world dataset of 157,525 cases spanning all 33 Orphanet categories and more than 7,000 conditions, RareLens outperformed every frontier model tested, including GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet and Gemini-2.5-Pro, across all stages. It achieved AUC 0.917 for screening and top-1 accuracies of 65.5% and 89.8% for diagnosis and treatment. In an external evaluation involving 1,287 cases and 23 physicians, autonomous RareLens and physicians assisted by RareLens both outperformed unaided physicians, while demonstrating that effective human-AI collaboration requires more than simply providing model outputs.

Three-State scoring distinguishes correct coverage, missing info, and incorrect claims. Errors get negative rather than zero credit. Ranks first on 6 of 9 benchmarks, achieves highest medical and generalization averages. Scores 38.98 on HealthBench-Hard vs InfiMed-ORBIT's 33.60 (8k samples) and 37.30 (28k samples). Uses 5,166-prompt rubric dataset.
relevance: Directly relevant to medical LLM benchmarking — introduces a novel RL training method using consensus rubrics, achieves SOTA on HealthBench-Hard. Part of the rapidly evolving medical LLM evaluation landscape.
key_findings: Ranks first on 6 of 9 benchmarks with highest medical and generalization averages
Scores 38.98 ± 1.04 on HealthBench-Hard, beating InfiMed-ORBIT (33.60 with 8k samples, 37.30 with 28k)
Consensus rubric approach — 3 LMs propose criteria, reviewer retains only cross-supported ones
Three-State scoring: correct coverage, missing info, incorrect claims (errors get negative credit)
5,166-prompt rubric dataset released
scale: 5,166 prompts, 9 benchmarks, HealthBench-Hard evaluation

title: Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing
authors: Lena Holzwarth et al.
abstract: Estimates LLM usage in biomedical publications using a new unbiased approach based on changing word frequencies. Analyzes full texts of open-access biomedical papers from PubMed Central. By end of 2025, 89% of papers show excess LLM-associated vocabulary. LLMs twice as likely in Discussion sections (68%) vs Methods sections (32%). Even in Methods, overall prevalence exceeds 50%. Findings crucial for shaping future guidelines and policies around LLM-assisted academic writing.
relevance: Critical context for evidence-based medicine platforms like OE — if 89% of biomedical publications show LLM-altered text, this affects the trustworthiness of the underlying evidence base that CDS tools rely on.
key_findings: 89% of open-access biomedical papers show excess LLM-associated vocabulary by end of 2025
Discussion sections: 68% LLM usage vs Methods sections: 32%
Even Methods sections show >50% LLM usage overall
New unbiased estimation method based on changing word frequencies
scale: Full PubMed Central open-access corpus

title: ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment
authors: Faik B Tek et al.
abstract: Presents ECHO (Enhanced Care & Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for chronic care management. Built on ReAct loop with LangGraph, 17 clinical tools, and temporal knowledge graph for cross-session memory. 94.9% tool-execution pass rate across 59 scenarios with GPT-5 Mini. Two-stage hybrid safety layer: rule-based (<1ms) + signed GNN with APPNP propagation (88.8% accuracy, 90.6% unsafe recall on 2,537-query Turkish health dataset). Multimodal speech assessment for emotion, depression, pain (macro F1 0.652). Runs on consumer hardware, GDPR/KVKK compliant.
relevance: Relevant to clinical AI tool landscape — demonstrates a fully local, agentic health assistant with novel hybrid safety architecture (rule-based + GNN). The local deployment angle and safety layer design are differentiators from cloud-based tools like OE.
key_findings: 94.9% tool-execution pass rate across 59 clinical scenarios with GPT-5 Mini
Two-stage safety: rule-based (<1ms) + signed GNN (88.8% accuracy, 90.6% unsafe recall)
Multimodal speech assessment: emotion, depression, pain (macro F1 0.652)
17 clinical tools, temporal knowledge graph for cross-session memory
Fully local on consumer hardware — GDPR/KVKK compliant

title: Conversation as Measurement in Clinical Encounters: Observable Phase Structure, Partially Observable Patient State
authors: Lily Chen et al.
abstract: Studies observability — whether targets are recoverable from conversational transcripts alone — in clinical encounters. Uses 439 real-world clinical encounter transcripts (134 hours), including 245 ENT transcripts paired with 273 PROM surveys. Finds an observability asymmetry: phase structure is observable and useful for characterizing encounter organization, while patient state is only partially observable even in settings designed to elicit symptoms. Uses PHI-compliant GPT-5 deployment for annotation with 40 hours of manual validation. COLM 2026.
relevance: Relevant to clinical AI evaluation methodology — demonstrates that transcript-only inference of patient state is unreliable, with implications for AI systems that analyze clinical conversations.
key_findings: Observability asymmetry: phase structure observable, patient state only partially observable
439 clinical encounter transcripts, 134 hours, 245 ENT + 273 PROM surveys
PHI-compliant GPT-5 deployment for annotation, 40 hours manual validation
Caution against transcript-only inference of human state
scale: 439 transcripts, 134 hours, 273 PROM surveys

title: Similarity Gates Approve Reversals: A Validity Audit of Embedding-Cosine Thresholds in Agent Systems
authors: Scott Frias et al.
abstract: Audits embedding-cosine similarity gates used in agent frameworks (deduplication, semantic caches, drift guards, answer graders). Shows these gates measure wording change, not meaning change — reversals can be single-word edits while paraphrases rephrase entire sentences. A production drift guard caught 0 of 56 meaning-breaking mutations. One approved item: 'withhold the study drug' → 'administer the study drug' at cosine 0.9608. Balanced accuracy never exceeded 0.700 across 90 cells. Strongest 2 of 9 configurations separated reversal from paraphrase at AUROC 0.79-0.90, but only with matched-pair audit.
relevance: Critical safety finding for clinical AI agent systems — demonstrates that embedding-cosine similarity gates (widely used in production) can approve meaning-reversing changes including clinical instructions ('withhold' → 'administer study drug'). Relevant to any RAG or agent-based clinical AI tool.

'withhold the study drug' → 'administer the study drug' approved at cosine 0.9608

Naively built evaluation corpus can return inverted verdict (AUROC 0.000 in 13/18 cells)

title: A corpus-specific clinical RAG system matches or outperforms newer frontier LLMs on HealthBench
authors: Praveen Reddy, Charuta Mandke, Suvrankar Datta, Sarah Khan, Siddharth Reddy Anthireddy, Shitij Arora, Vishal Singh
abstract: Evaluates VITA, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system purpose-built for contextual knowledge retrieval in India and other LMIC settings. VITA retrieves from a curated corpus of disease-specific guidelines, India-specific antimicrobial resistance data, national formulary constraints, and resource-limited care protocols. On 4,023 English-language HealthBench questions (80.5% of the benchmark), scored with a GPT-4.1 judge, VITA ranked first with 51.9% of possible rubric points, ahead of GPT-5.4 (46.1%), o4-mini (44.3%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (42.6%), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (37.3%). A 500-question subset re-run against current-generation models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Pro, Grok 4.3) and graded by a neutral open-weight judge (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) showed VITA and GPT-5.5 statistically indistinguishable on mean per-question score, while VITA led on points-weighted score and won the most questions.
relevance: Directly relevant: purpose-built clinical RAG system benchmarked against frontier LLMs on HealthBench — demonstrates corpus specificity as a design variable that improves grounding in clinical AI tools
key_findings: VITA (clinical RAG) ranked first on HealthBench with 51.9% rubric points vs GPT-5.4 (46.1%), o4-mini (44.3%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (42.6%), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (37.3%)
VITA scored highest on 45.4% of questions in the GPT-4.1 judged evaluation
Against newer models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Pro, Grok 4.3) with neutral judge (DeepSeek-V4-Pro), VITA and GPT-5.5 were statistically indistinguishable on mean per-question score
VITA led on points-weighted score and won the most questions even under neutral judge
Corpus specificity improves grounding accuracy but comes at cost of lower communication scores

title: Artificial intelligence in cardiovascular care: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
authors: Ong AQC, Ang CS, Bojic I, Johnson CL, Aggour H, Ng FS, Car J, Leeson P, Gonçalves J, Lai NM
abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 RCTs (n=1,685,717 patients) across 13 regions evaluating effectiveness of AI interventions in cardiovascular care. 71% of trials reported significant AI benefit on primary endpoints (mostly intermediate process measures); 29% showed no effect. Meta-analysis: image-based AI-CDSS reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.96; I²=0%); AI-mobile health reduced systolic BP (-3.18 mmHg). AI-ECG did not significantly improve heart failure detection. Certainty of evidence low to very low (GRADE) due to risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision.
relevance: High-quality Lancet-family meta-analysis pinning down real-world effectiveness of clinical AI decision support — pivotal benchmark evidence for the regulatory and adoption narrative around systems like OpenEvidence. Image-based AI-CDSS achieves 26% relative reduction in MACE; mobile AI works for BP; AI-ECG does not move hard outcomes.
key_findings: 31 RCTs, 1,685,717 patients, 13 regions — most comprehensive cardiovascular AI RCT review to date
71% of trials reported significant AI benefit, but mostly on intermediate process endpoints rather than hard outcomes
Image-based AI-CDSS reduced MACE (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.96; n=1,614,689 pooled subset)
AI-mobile health reduced systolic BP by 3.18 mmHg; no effect on diastolic BP or BMI
AI-enhanced ECG did not improve heart failure detection (RR 1.22, I²=90%)
Certainty low-to-very-low (GRADE) due to risk of bias and indirectness — limits translation to OE-style evidence lookup tools
scale: 31 RCTs, 1,685,717 patients, 13 regions; PROSPERO CRD420251090250

title: CARE: Confidence-Aware Reasoning for Reliable Medical VQA
authors: Yuetian Du, Yucheng Wang, Zhenyuan Chen, Luyuan Chen, Rongyu Zhang, Jinjian Zhang, Wei Zhou, Zhijie Xu, Ming Kong, Zhan Zhou, Jie Liu, Qiang Zhu
abstract: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has enabled medical Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) to produce Chain-of-Thought reasoning for visual question answering, yet they suffer from confidence miscalibration — a systematic gap between expressed certainty and actual diagnostic accuracy that undermines clinical trust. CARE is a Confidence-Aware REasoning framework that jointly optimizes accuracy and calibration via dual-stage pipeline (Medical-CoT SFT + GRPO with Confidence-Aware Reward). Across three Medical VQA benchmarks, CARE achieves highest diagnostic accuracy with lowest Expected Calibration Error and Hallucination Rate. (Accepted at MICCAI 2026)
relevance: Methodology for confidence-aware clinical VQA reasoning — directly relevant to clinical AI safety/calibration and OE-style physician-AI teaming at point of care
key_findings: Identifies confidence miscalibration as a systematic gap in medical MLLMs
Dual-stage pipeline: cold-start Medical-CoT SFT + GRPO with Confidence-Aware Reward tying confidence to correctness
Best diagnostic accuracy + lowest Expected Calibration Error (ECE) + lowest Hallucination Rate across 3 Medical VQA benchmarks
Frames CARE as foundation for trustworthy clinical decision support
Code released at github.com/anotherbricki/CARE
Accepted at MICCAI 2026
tools_evaluated: Medical MLLMs (general); benchmarks specific to paper
scale: 3 medical VQA benchmarks

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning for Hemodynamic Management of Sepsis in the ICU: a MIMIC-IV Study with Dual Off-Policy Evaluation
authors: Marc Pérez-Roig, David Fernández-Narro, Carlos Sáez
abstract: Models fluid and vasopressor dosing for sepsis on 36,872 MIMIC-IV ICU stays as a discretized MDP (1,000 states, 25 actions). Estimates clinician behavior policy with random forest, evaluates learned policy with WIS and FQE. Learned policy exceeds clinician return (WIS 50.8, FQE 46.8 vs 38.2) while departing modestly from observed practice (TV 0.18), favoring less IV fluid. Proposes discordance-based clinical decision-support approach for sepsis management.
relevance: Clinical decision support system for ICU hemodynamic management using RL with rigorous off-policy evaluation — directly relevant to CDSS methodology.

title: ETHOS: Towards a Modular Ethics Framework for Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Rakesh Sharma, Sydney Pugh, Cameron Beeche, Pankhuri Singhal, Rachel Wu, Margaret Eby, Jeffrey Duda, James Gee, Kyra O'Brien, Hersh Sagreiya, Marina Serper, Victoria Gershuni, Angela Bradbury, Anurag Verma, Eric Eaton, Kevin B. Johnson, Walter Witschey
abstract: Modular ethics framework (ETHOS) designed as a governance meta-agent integrable into any clinical multi-agent system without architectural changes. Translates ethical requirements into runtime oversight via deterministic checks, contextual reviews, and a final ethics critic. Demonstrated in hepatology clinical decision-support MAS — improves decision reliability by detecting incomplete, inconsistent, or out-of-scope evidence and increasing abstention when safe recommendations cannot be supported.
journal: arXiv preprint (cs.MA, cs.AI) — submitted to Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing 2027
relevance: Practical ethics governance framework for clinical multi-agent AI systems — directly addresses safety oversight in clinical decision support.

title: Demographic Injection in Medical Language Models under Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Prompts
authors: Diego Mardian, Frank Liu
abstract: Shows that a one-sentence DEI prompt appended to medical questions causes 47 LLMs to inject patient demographic attributes (race, SES, sex) the question never stated — raising injection rate from 0.7% to 33.1% (47x) across 47 models, 4 medical benchmarks, and 376,000 responses. A smaller subset (0.25-2.4%) attaches invented demographics to specific patients or changes the selected answer, 99.8% toward the incorrect option. Demonstrates a general mechanism: any instruction nudging model reasoning can introduce unrequested patient details that alter clinical recommendations.
relevance: Large-scale evaluation across 47 models and 4 medical benchmarks revealing a novel safety failure mode in medical LLMs — directly relevant to clinical AI safety and benchmarking.

title: Removing Temporal Note Redundancy Improves Multimodal Reinforcement Learning for Medicine
authors: Chenran Weng, Joo Seung Lee, Malini Mahendra, Anil Aswani
abstract: Proposes redundancy-aware multimodal state representation for RL in mechanical ventilation management. Removes temporal note redundancy (copy-forward, templating) via embedding-space SVD decomposition and sentence-level diffing before policy learning. Using real ICU data, stripped-redundancy representations significantly outperform structured-only and raw-note baselines across multiple off-policy evaluation methods (MBR, FQE, WIS, WDR). Shows that isolating new clinical information from repeated note text improves RL performance for clinical decision support.
relevance: Clinical decision support methodology improvement — demonstrates that temporal redundancy removal in clinical notes improves RL-based CDSS performance.

title: Generated Context versus Governed State: Functional Conditions for Accountable Longitudinal Clinical Reasoning
authors: Augusto Bernardo Pissarra, Victor Lorena de Farias Souza
abstract: Argues that longitudinal clinical reasoning is a state-estimation problem under partial observability, and that the axis on which clinical AI succeeds or fails is not the fluency of the model reading the record but the governance of the patient state it reasons over. Distinguishes generated context from governed state; separates five objects that clinical AI habitually conflates (true state, observations, evidence, belief, and simulated state); defines a tiered governance standard against which any clinical AI system can be audited; and shows that an operational definition of accountability decomposes into four information requirements: an immutable evidence ledger with awareness-time versioning, a belief state distinct from accumulated evidence, an observation-process model, and claim-level causal typing. A six-level maturity framework locates current LLM-centric practice at high capability but low maturity.
relevance: Conceptual framework for clinical AI accountability and governance — directly relevant to evaluating how clinical AI tools like OpenEvidence maintain and govern patient state over time. The six-level maturity framework provides an audit instrument for current LLM-centric clinical AI systems.

title: Improving Rural Medication Safety with AI: A Scoping Review
authors: Ashad Kabir
abstract: Scoping review of 12 primary studies from 9 nations examining AI applications for medication safety in rural healthcare settings (2012-2025). AI technologies including Clinical Decision Support Systems, Machine Learning, NLP, and smart pumps were integrated across prescribing, dispensing, administration, and monitoring. ML-based surveillance improved incident detection and reduced prescribing/transcription errors by 34-80%. Barriers included lack of governance frameworks, financial limitations, clinician resistance, and alert fatigue. AI technologies hold potential for enhancing pharmaceutical safety in rural healthcare through data-driven monitoring, automated processes, and clinical decision assistance.
relevance: Directly relevant to clinical AI decision support tools — evaluates CDSS and AI applications for medication safety in resource-limited settings, a key deployment context for tools like OpenEvidence.

title: RareLens: Towards End-to-End Rare Disease Care via Aligning Divergent Large Language Model Reasoning
authors: Xi Chen, Hongru Zhou, Shiyu Feng, Hanyu Zhou, Huahui Yi, Rongsheng Wang, Tiancheng He, Kun Wang, Pingping Liu, Qiankun Li, Sicheng Lin, Huiying Ou, Xiaohong Zheng, Tianying Zang, Zhuohang Wu, Leheng Jiang, Kexin Cao, Wenhan Zhang, ChengYi Li, Zhiyang Wang, Songlin Li, Benyou Wang, Ningbei Yin, Shaoting Zhang, Weili Fu, Jian Li, Kang Li
abstract: Exploits diversity of multiple imperfect LLM reasoning systems for rare disease clinical decision-making. Identifies divergent reasoning trajectories with complementary error patterns across heterogeneous LLMs and develops RareLens, which reconciles these perspectives into actionable decisions across four stages: risk screening, diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis prediction. Built on RarelensBench (157,525 cases, 33 Orphanet categories, 7,000+ conditions). RareLens outperformed GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and Gemini-2.5-Pro across all stages. External evaluation with 1,287 cases and 23 physicians showed autonomous RareLens and physician+RareLens both outperformed unaided physicians.
relevance: Highly relevant — multi-LLM ensemble approach for clinical decision support across full care pathway. RarelensBench benchmarks frontier models on rare disease care. Physician-AI teaming evaluation with 23 physicians directly comparable to OpenEvidence's clinical AI deployment model.

title: Multidisciplinary dental treatment planning by artificial intelligence: A comparative evaluation
authors: Kazim SA, Alnoman BA, Hashim RM, Goodacre CJ
abstract: Comparative evaluation of four AI programs - ChatGPT-5, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini (v2.5) and OpenEvidence - in generating comprehensive dental treatment plans for minimally destructed and severely mutilated teeth. Ten anonymized clinical cases (1 intraoral photograph + 1 periapical radiograph each) submitted to each system with a standardized prompt; reference standard set by consensus of four calibrated specialists (prosthodontist, restorative dentist, surgically trained prosthodontist, endodontist). Structured rubric across five domains (diagnostic accuracy, restorability assessment, multidisciplinary integration, treatment sequencing, extraction appropriateness; 0-10 per case); inter-evaluator agreement kappa=0.74 (95% CI 0.68-0.80). Mean total scores: OpenEvidence 7.7+/-1.4, ChatGPT-5 7.6+/-1.1, Gemini 5.1+/-1.2, Copilot 4.7+/-3.1 (Copilot failed 3/10 cases due to content filtering). OpenEvidence and ChatGPT-5 more frequently incorporated phased sequencing, ferrule assessment, restorability analysis and multidisciplinary considerations. Clinically significant diagnostic errors observed across all systems; authors recommend AI plans be treated as adjunctive decision support requiring specialist oversight.
relevance: Direct four-way head-to-head of OpenEvidence vs general-purpose AI on multidisciplinary dental treatment planning against specialist consensus
key_findings: OpenEvidence achieved the highest mean score (7.7+/-1.4), edging ChatGPT-5 (7.6+/-1.1); Gemini 5.1+/-1.2; Copilot 4.7+/-3.1
Microsoft Copilot failed to generate responses for 3 of 10 cases due to content-filtering restrictions
OpenEvidence and ChatGPT-5 more frequently incorporated phased treatment sequencing, ferrule assessment, restorability analysis and multidisciplinary considerations
Substantial inter-evaluator agreement (Cohen's kappa=0.74, 95% CI 0.68-0.80)
Clinically significant diagnostic errors observed across all systems - AI plans should remain adjunctive with specialist oversight
scale: 10 clinical cases, 4 AI systems, 4 calibrated specialists, 5-domain rubric

title: Vocal Cord Dysfunction: Evaluating the Utility of AI Large Language Models for Patient Education
authors: Cook K, Tseng P, Ahmadian D, Demirjian N, Liu V, Weinstein T, Yip H
abstract: Cross-sectional survey comparing provider preferences for patient education materials on vocal cord dysfunction (VCD) generated by OpenEvidence, ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking, and a fellowship-trained laryngologist. Four common VCD patient questions; expert responses authored by the laryngologist; AI responses generated with a standardized role prompt limited to four sentences. 45 healthcare providers (mostly otolaryngology n=17 and allergy/immunology n=12; 31 attendings) ranked responses on medical accuracy, clarity, and addressing patient concerns (chi-square goodness-of-fit + Friedman with post hoc pairwise comparisons). ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking received the most first-choice selections for 3 of 4 questions; OpenEvidence and ChatGPT performed similarly on the definition question. Significant differences among sources for all four questions (all Friedman p<=0.001): AI responses preferred over the laryngologist response for definition, diagnosis, and treatment-process questions; ChatGPT preferred over both comparators for etiology. Supports LLMs as adjunctive patient-education tools in laryngology with clinician oversight.
journal: World Journal of Otorhinolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
relevance: Head-to-head of OpenEvidence vs ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking vs expert-authored patient education materials, ranked by 45 clinicians
key_findings: AI-generated responses were preferred over the fellowship-trained laryngologist's response for definition, diagnosis and treatment-process questions
ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking performed best overall (most first-choice selections on 3 of 4 questions)
OpenEvidence performed comparably to ChatGPT on the definition question and on several other items
Significant differences among sources for all four questions (all Friedman p<=0.001)
Supports LLMs as adjunctive patient-education tools with clinician oversight and patient-outcome studies
scale: 4 patient questions, 3 sources, 45 healthcare provider raters

title: The Role of Large Language Models in Hormonal Contraception Consultation
authors: Psilopatis I, Emons J, Zwimpfer TA
abstract: Background: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate promise in medical applications, but their performance in hormonal contraception consultation remains underexplored. Objective: To evaluate the accuracy and comprehensiveness of LLM-generated hormonal contraception counseling compared to evidence-based guidelines. Methods: Ten fictitious clinical case scenarios representing common contraceptive counseling situations were presented to Chat-GPT, Google Gemini, and OpenEvidence. Cases assessed medical eligibility screening, contraindication recognition, drug interactions, side effect management, and emergency contraception guidance. Two board-certified obstetrician-gynecologists independently evaluated the responses based on international clinical guidelines. Results: Across the ten predefined clinical scenarios, all three LLMs achieved high accuracy in identifying contraindications according to Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) and provided appropriate alternative contraceptive recommendations. Models demonstrated high proficiency in managing drug interactions, particularly the lamotrigine-estrogen interaction, and provided evidence-based side effect management strategies. However, the communication styles differed. Chat-GPT emphasized structured consultation and shared decision-making, Gemini provided practical action-oriented guidance, and OpenEvidence delivered concise evidence-focused summaries. Conclusions: In this limited set of standardized fictitious cases, the evaluated LLMs generally provided responses that were broadly aligned with selected guideline recommendations. Current LLMs require cautious deployment, given limitations in individualized assessment and health literacy optimization, and are best positioned as complementary educational tools rather than replacements for professional contraceptive counseling.
relevance: Evaluates accuracy and comprehensiveness of OpenEvidence, ChatGPT and Gemini for hormonal contraception counseling against evidence-based guidelines
key_findings: Ten fictitious contraceptive counseling cases covering eligibility screening, contraindication recognition, drug interactions, side-effect management and emergency contraception
Outputs independently rated by two board-certified obstetrician-gynecologists against evidence-based guidelines
scale: 10 clinical case scenarios, 3 LLMs, 2 board-certified OB-GYN raters

title: Right Diagnoses, Decorative Reasoning: A Perturbation Audit of Medical Chain-of-Thought
authors: Mengzhu Xu, Jifan Gao, Xia Jiang, Yaoxin Wu, Xi Long
abstract: Clinicians read chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales as evidence of medical reasoning, but whether the visible chain plays that role is rarely tested. We close this gap with a medical perturbation audit: a 30-operator battery edits both the chain and the question with clinically motivated operators (severity reversal, negation flip, demographic swap, evidence ablation), paired with a chain-update times answer-flip joint analysis. Applied to 14 LLMs on four medical QA benchmarks, three independent tests converge: the Chain-Decoupling Rate (CDR) is 72.9% panel-wide on clinically meaningful destructive edits, chain corruption leaves accuracy unchanged, and removing CoT prompting does not reduce accuracy. Two board-certified clinicians re-annotate N=197 perturbed questions; 98.5% leave the gold defensible.
relevance: Directly evaluates clinical AI safety by auditing whether chain-of-thought reasoning in medical LLMs is faithful or merely decorative. Introduces the Chain-Decoupling Rate (CDR) as a reusable yardstick. 14 LLMs tested on 4 medical QA benchmarks including MedQA.
key_findings: 72.9% Chain-Decoupling Rate — chain does not register clinically meaningful edits and answer does not flip
Chain corruption leaves accuracy unchanged, removing CoT prompting does not reduce accuracy
Pattern holds across medical and reasoning fine-tuning and scale
Two board-certified clinicians confirm 98.5% of gold answers remain defensible after perturbation
tools_evaluated: 14 LLMs (panel including medical and general-purpose models)
scale: 14 LLMs, 4 medical QA benchmarks, 197 clinician-annotated perturbed questions

title: SDoH-Aware Narrative Anchoring Bias in Medical LLMs for Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support
authors: Ahnaf Atef Choudhury, Ramkrishna Saha
abstract: Medical LLMs may know the right answer and still change their response when the same case is written in a different patient voice. This paper evaluates SDoH-aware narrative anchoring bias using NarrativeShield SDoH MedQA, a counterfactual medical QA dataset. Three open-source LLMs from the Qwen2.5 family (1.5B, 3B, 7B) were evaluated. 300 clinical cases produce 8,100 model responses. Qwen2.5 7B achieves best accuracy at 56.33% and correct consistency at 40.33%. Lowest narrative sensitivity error still at 31.67%.
relevance: Directly evaluates clinical decision support safety by measuring whether medical LLMs change answers based on patient narrative voice rather than clinical content. Introduces narrative sensitivity error metric.
key_findings: 31.67% narrative sensitivity error — models change answers when same case written in different patient voice
Qwen2.5 7B: 56.33% accuracy, 40.33% correct consistency
Paired McNemar tests show significant accuracy gains for 7B over 3B in all prompt settings
Trustworthy clinical decision support requires evaluating stability across medically equivalent patient narratives
scale: 300 clinical cases, 8,100 model responses, 3 prompting conditions

title: Performance of a domain-specific large language model in answering patient questions in psychiatry
authors: Alexander J. Hish, Arjun Nagendran, Scott N. Compton
abstract: Evaluates whether a domain-specific LLM (MIND) fine-tuned on patient education resources can answer questions about psychiatric medications better than LLM chatbots. Compares MIND, ChatGPT, and OpenEvidence on patient questions about escitalopram. When rated by rubric, MIND was highest in all domains (p<0.001). When rated by 10 board-licensed psychiatrists, ChatGPT was rated accurate more often than MIND (negligible effect size), MIND was rated complete more often (small effect size). 57.6% of psychiatrists preferred ChatGPT responses vs 42.4% MIND (p=0.003).
relevance: Directly evaluates OpenEvidence alongside ChatGPT and a domain-specific LLM (MIND) in psychiatry. One of the few studies comparing OpenEvidence to other tools in a specific clinical specialty.
key_findings: MIND rated highest by rubric in all domains (accuracy, clarity, completeness, nuance, safety, referral appropriateness)
Psychiatrists preferred ChatGPT (57.6%) over MIND (42.4%, p=0.003)
MIND rated more complete than ChatGPT (small effect size, p<0.001)
MIND and ChatGPT rated safe with same frequency (p=0.955)
OpenEvidence included in comparison but not top-rated
scale: Patient questions about escitalopram, 10 board-licensed psychiatrists

title: Teaching LLMs How ICU Physicians Approach Clinical Reasoning Through OMOP-Aligned Retrieval Improves Reasoning Across Clinical Domains
authors: Miguel Contreras, Scott Siegel, Subhash Nerella, Jessica Sena, Jiaqing Zhang, Heng Sun, et al.
abstract: Introduces ICU-REACT, a reasoning dataset developed with 19 clinicians through a clinician-in-the-loop framework to teach LLMs information retrieval and context-aware clinical reasoning in the ICU. Fine-tuned Clin-REACT models (8B-70B, three model families) consistently outperformed backbone models and open-source general-purpose and medical LLMs across five clinical reasoning benchmarks. Gains extended to script concordance tests and downstream diagnosis/treatment tasks.
relevance: RAG-based clinical AI evaluation — demonstrates that expert reasoning supervision in critical care improves broader clinical reasoning. Directly relevant to OpenEvidence's RAG architecture and clinical decision support approach.
key_findings: Clin-REACT models outperformed backbone models across 5 clinical reasoning benchmarks
Gains extended to script concordance tests and downstream diagnosis/treatment tasks
Expert ICU reasoning supervision generalizes beyond critical care
19 clinicians contributed to dataset through clinician-in-the-loop framework
scale: 19 clinicians, 5 clinical reasoning benchmarks, 8B-70B parameter models

title: Benchmarking Clinical Decision Pathway Adherence in Large Language Models
authors: Nuo Chen, Xinyang Jiang, Zilong Wang, Zhifei Zhang, Xiaoye Qu, Jiajun Deng, Yulan Guo, Cairong Zhao
abstract: Following clinical decision pathways (CDPs) defined by clinical practice guidelines is essential for safe and reliable medical decision-making. However, existing medical large language model (LLM) benchmarks mainly evaluate final-answer accuracy, providing limited evaluation of models' ability to adhere to guidelines. To address this gap, we introduce MEGA-CDP, a benchmark for evaluating whether medical LLMs can generate guideline-adherent CDPs using provided guidelines as references. MEGA-CDP is constructed from 2,274 English and Chinese clinical practice guidelines through a guideline-to-case pipeline, yielding 42,353 clinical cases with explicit reference CDPs. It supports both single-turn vignette and multi-turn interactive settings, and introduces a CDP-oriented evaluation framework for measuring pathway consistency. Experiments on 16 representative LLMs show that reliable clinical decision support remains challenging for current models, demonstrating the need for CDP-oriented evaluation and the value of MEGA-CDP for advancing guideline adherence in medical LLMs.
relevance: high
key_findings: Introduces MEGA-CDP, a benchmark with 42,353 clinical cases from 2,274 guidelines evaluating whether medical LLMs can generate guideline-adherent clinical decision pathways. Tests 16 LLMs in single-turn and multi-turn settings. Finds that reliable clinical decision support remains challenging for current models.
tools_evaluated: 16 representative LLMs (unspecified which specific clinical AI tools)
scale: 42,353 clinical cases from 2,274 English and Chinese clinical practice guidelines
